items.title: Ray Gunn Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Ray Gunn opens in select theaters on December 4 and arrives on Netflix on December 18. The film premiered on October 10 at the London Film Festival.

A 30-odd-year passion project for director Brad Bird, is a nifty sci-fi/film noir mashup that’s sumptuously designed and cleverly realized, but is slightly dinged by an overlong runtime and occasionally clunky story.

Set in the vast futuristic city of Metropia, Ray Gunn follows its titular private eye (voiced by Sam Rockwell) as he and his one-eyed alien partner, Eye-Ra (Tom Waits), investigate a case involving the world’s biggest pop star, Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), that leads to murder, corruption and other nefarious things. If that sounds pretty gritty for an animated film from the director of The Incredibles and Ratatouille, it is.

Ray Gunn definitely leans toward a slightly older demographic than the broader audience of Bird’s past films for Pixar, which is perfectly fine since animation can obviously be more than just one kind of movie made specifically for children. While it may not be a zany animated comedy for the whole family, Ray Gunn still offers its share of cartoon hijinks for anyone who does watch it with their kids. Ray’s particle blaster pistol yields some raucous moments that would otherwise be considered body horror in a more serious film, and there’s a little alien version of essentially a French bulldog that satisfies the cute factor.

The alien designs are rather familiar but appropriate for the world these characters inhabit. The film uses some of these alien designs for humor and utility, such as Eye-Ra’s spider-like climbing skills. Other aliens are homages to film noir characters. The Jabba-like crime lord Slugsy is clearly patterned after The Maltese Falcon and Casablanca actor Sydney Greenstreet while his little henchman looks and sounds just like Peter Lorre.

The aliens who inhabit Metropia also serve as the film’s metaphor for a world where segregation and xenophobia still exist but are applied to aliens instead of humans. Aliens do all the manual labor and are banned from entering certain human facilities (for example, aliens must go to their own hospitals). There were even more avenues Ray Gunn could’ve taken to explore these serious issues a bit deeper. Unfortunately, the most noteworthy discussion about how the film explores its metaphor for racism can’t be discussed here due to major spoilers, but it was something different than an animated movie has broached before and the film handles it thoughtfully.

Ray Gunn drags a bit in the middle as the story winds its ways through the requisite beats of a detective procedural, trying to misdirect the viewer on things and characters that seemed rather obvious all along. The film, especially during its homestretch, also packs in a lot of under-explored messaging about the entertainment industry, technology and human nature without delving deeply enough to explore any of those topics beyond the cursory.

On a technical level, Ray Gunn boasts a stellar retro-futuristic aesthetic across the board, from its architecture to its costumes and gizmos and vehicles. This is a beautiful looking and sounding film (one that was especially enjoyable in a Dolby theater, so it’s a shame that most people probably won’t discover Ray Gunn until it lands on Netflix).

Composer Michael Giacchino’s moody score sounds exactly like one you’d hear in a 1940s movie, especially during more dialogue-driven or romantic scenes. All of the creative elements make Ray Gunn pulpy fun with an old-school sci-fi gloss.

The voice cast are uniformly solid across the board, with Rockwell leading the pack as the hardboiled but glib gumshoe who somehow holds on to his optimism. The cynicism that’s inherent in film noir is provided here by Eye-Ra, who Waits plays with just the right mix of world-weariness and wry wit. Matt Berry is suitably erudite but sleazy as the voice of Slugsy, while Bobby Canavale, Alan Tudyk, Michelle Rodriguez and Kether Donohue all get their respective moments to shine in supporting roles.

And it should come as no surprise that Scarlett Johansson lends a breathy sultriness to the film’s femme fatale Venus Nova, but what might surprise you is how fine of a singer she is. Composer Kimbra provides three songs for the film that Johansson performs, with “Innocent” being the biggest earworm of the group.

items.title: Soylent Green Blu-ray Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
It’s the United States of the 2020s. Climate change has created a perpetual heat wave, pollution has contaminated the air, and overpopulation combined with the consolidation of wealth and power in the hands of a select and self-interested few has resulted in major cities becoming seas of human bodies with no space and barely any resources to live. The elite can still access clean water and fresh food, but they live under guard in isolated palatial homes with women who are deprived of autonomy. The rest eat food increasingly processed and surely riddled with pathogens, and intellect and education has been eradicated for the masses, with only the elderly recalling the value of reading and academia.

So I thought: Why not watch an old favorite film instead of focusing on the real world like this? Thanks to Arrow Video, I can, through this new 4K UHD and Blu-ray release. “What is the secret of Soylent Green?” is the question asked of everyone that saw the trailer for this Charlton Heston-starring dystopian sci-fi classic way back in 1973 (concluding an apocalyptic “trilogy” for Heston that began with 1968’s and 1971’s ). But can anyone in 2026 come to this film knowing the crucial revelation upon which the entire plot relies? Maybe, since we’re now in such a fragmented era of media consumption, with people far less likely to watch the same things, not to mention that there’s even more of a tendency to ignore the old in favor of the new. If fresh eyes fall on , they may just be surprised, and I don’t want to do anything to rob them of that experience. So believe it or not, no spoilers here; it may be a futile effort, but if anyone makes any obvious jokes or references in the comments below, at least it won’t be me.

I Think It's Really Busted This Time

Charlton Heston called Soylent Green “the best B movie ever made,” but it’s so much more. At its most fundamental, the film is a noirish police procedural with a hard-bitten detective, a damsel in distress, and a global conspiracy that’s bigger than both of them. A board member of the Soylent corporation — supplier of processed food wafers like the new Soylent Green, made from plankton — named Simonson (Joseph Cotten in a very brief appearance) has been brutally murdered, and Robert Thorn (Heston) is assigned to crack the case. Police work is completely corrupt, however, so Thorn spends more time lifting luxuries from Simonson’s opulent pad and availing himself of the “furniture,” otherwise known as Shirl (Leigh Taylor-Young) — one of the many women in this world whose life has been reduced to domestic imprisonment and sexual servitude in apartments occupied by their elite masters. With Simonson dead, Shirl will soon meet the new tenant that she’ll be required to serve; for now, at least, she has Thorn.

This is a relentlessly moist movie; to convey the oppressive levels of heat, the entire cast is drenched in stage sweat except when in the domains of the wealthy (and a certain elderly-centered facility late in the film). The movie is also largely drab and awash in beiges and grays, but the color palette pops when necessary with bright saturated colors that really shine on this new release, whether it’s a rare strawberry or a blue dress. It looks beautiful and rich, but with a grain that feels right for the period; I’m not sure if it was always there, but there’s an additional haze that looks particularly appropriate and oppressive whenever we’re outside in the heat, with a greenish tint that reminds us Soylent Green is omnipresent.

The movie is also a masterclass in world-building, beginning with a montage created by Charles Braverman (based on his 1968 short film, “American Time Capsule”). With bombastic music by Fred Myrow (whose scoring is kept minimal in the rest of the film), the rapid-fire depiction of the country’s industrial development and degradation sets the Soylent-laden stage. Opening scenes set in Thorn’s apartment juxtaposed with the home of the wealthy Simonson perfectly delineate the ways in which the two main tiers of society operate in this far-flung future of 2022, as well as the kinds of relationships that define their lives.

(And yes, Star Trek: Deep Space Nine drew on this concept for their two-part episode, “Past Tense,” and even referenced soylent in prop posters. And yes, the film’s co-star Brock Peters is Sisko’s dad on DS9. Moving on…)

We've Gotta Stop Them… Somehow

Despite being part of a deeply damaged system, there’s a nobility to Heston’s Thorn and a dedication to the truth that drives him to actually do his job. Much of that comes from his long-term father-son relationship with his “book,” Solomon Roth (Edward G. Robinson), an elderly former college professor and live-in research assistant who provides Thorn with crucial investigative support. Their bond provides the emotional core of the movie, no doubt at least partially informed by their previous work together in The Ten Commandments (1956) and the original makeup tests for Planet of the Apes, where Robinson played Zaius (he dropped out of the actual film for health reasons). Thorn’s relationship with Chief Hatcher (Brock Peters) is another great touch. Hatcher relies on his colleague and friend to regularly fix his watch, and Thorn tinkers away, thus letting us know he’s rather smart for this world too… but only to a point. When he finally admits he can no longer repair the watch, it’s symbolic of something much larger; there are some things that will be beyond his ability to fix.

The moment when Thorn hears the secret of Soylent Green (but the audience doesn’t yet) from Sol himself and is moved to tears will haunt you for days afterward.

The film features a solid supporting cast that all add so much to even the smallest roles, including former Rifleman Chuck Connors as bodyguard Tab, the mesmerizing Paula Kelly as Tab’s girlfriend (roommate?) Martha, and the unctuous Leonard Stone as the apartment manager/pimp, Charles. In particular, fellow Omega Man alum Lincoln Kilpatrick turns up as Paul, a priest with knowledge that’s eating him away from within, and he even gets to reference the title of the 1966 Harry Harrison novel that serves as this film’s inspiration, Make Room! Make Room! Celia Lovsky (Vulcan matriarch T’Pau from the Star Trek original series episode “Amok Time”) also appears as the leader of the Exchange, where Sol and other “books” meet to share sources and information. She gets to tee up the obligatory “is Chuck actually God” joke, and when Sol brings her a rare volume never seen by the Exchange before, her trembling hands reaching reverently for the cover of the book is so evocative of everything that’s been lost.

But in many ways, this is Robinson’s film. A scene in which he eats real food with such relish and then realizes how profoundly sad it is that they’ve come to this state is a study in expertly modulated acting. The veteran actor knew he was dying even as he completed his last role — he passed away two months after finishing filming — and he brings every bit of experience and pain to a beautiful performance that also seems to push Heston to up his game. As a bookend to the film’s expertly-crafted opening, the film’s finale is a harrowing journey to the truth that begins when Sol makes a fateful decision that leads him and Thorn to the conclusion of the investigation and the movie’s big reveal. There’s a moment during that final sequence, when Thorn hears the secret of Soylent Green (but the audience doesn’t ) from Sol himself and is moved to tears; it will haunt you for days afterward.

While there is a new 2025 commentary track recorded for Arrow with film historian Michael Brooke and author Johnny Mains, there aren’t many other extras here you wouldn’t have encountered in previous releases of the film, including image galleries, the trailer, vintage featurettes about the making of the movie and its landmark position as Robinson’s 101st film, and an archival 2003 commentary track with director Richard Fleischer and actress Leigh Taylor-Young. Fleischer covers the thematic and production elements, while Taylor-Young chimes in to discuss her environmental work at the UN, her view of the film as a “harbinger,” and her attempt at a Ten Commandments joke during her shower scene with Heston. You can hear Heston briefly discuss the film during an audio-only 1985 BFI appearance, while Fleischer touches on it in a 1994 BFI interview captured on video that also covers his memories of the blacklisting era.

Perhaps most significant, however, in terms of additions for this new release is a booklet presenting material written by Dr. Alexandra Heller-Nicholas (who I recently encountered via her superb contributions to Severin Films’ Sangster Directs Hammer box set). I’d to tell you more about it, but I , because Arrow didn’t provide an actual release copy for review. It was very nice to at least receive the screener disc, but as these reviews are about celebrating and supporting physical releases, that includes all aspects of the presentation. I have to assume Dr. Nichols’ work is exemplary as always; her attention to detail and respect for history is surely better than Arrow’s, which sent an accompanying press release listing other classic ’70s sci-fi films “Wetworld” and “The Andromeda Syndrome.” JFC, Arrow.

items.title: Avatar: Seven Havens Episodes 1-3 Recap and Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
This review contains full spoilers for Season 1, Episodes 1-3, which debut October 9 on Paramount+.

The experience of watching the first new Avatar series in 12 years — Avatar Aang movie and Netflix’s live-action adaptation aside — is an overwhelming one. While there have been numerous (pretty excellent) comic book tie-ins and extensions released in the intervening decade plus, insuring that the world created by Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko has never fully gone away, they’ve all felt like mere footsteps from the stellar runs of Avatar: The Last Airbender and The Legend of Korra — reinterpretations of information we already had on hand instead of something really new.

Avatar: Seven Havens, on the other hand, really truly new. Set 225 years after the events of Legend of Korra in a post-apocalyptic landscape where all that remains of humanity is based in the Seven Havens of the title, the show evolves the animation style and setting in a way that’s closer to Miyazaki or recent surreal hits like Scavengers Reign or Common Side Effects rather than what we might expect from an Avatar series.

But even with the different animation, there’s something both alien and familiar about watching Seven Havens. On one hand, you’ve got a kid Avatar in Pavi (Saheli Khan) — more on that in a second — just like Aang in the original series. But unlike Aang, who had a very clear path forward (stop the Fire Lord, save the world), Pavi has been living on the outskirts with only bugs, rocks, and her cat-monkey (voiced by Dee Bradley Baker, the voice of Appa and Momo in the original series) as friends, with no clear path to saving a world that maybe doesn’t to be saved.

The sly humor that DiMartino and Konietzko have woven into previous series is back, and an early sequence in the premiere, “On The Horizon,” with Jae (Major Curda) surfing his way through the Haven of Ellora is an utter delight. But if Korra took the franchise in darker, more adult directions, Seven Havens is both a reflection of the world we live in today and of the anger some fans felt toward the character of Korra. The plot involves something Korra did two centuries earlier that broke the world, leading to the survivors hating and fearing the Avatar; it’s also clear in the first three episodes that this story isn’t done, and it also isn’t what the world thinks. It’s just speculation, but it very much feels like DiMartino and Konietzko are saying, “Oh, you hate Korra so much? Well, here’s why you’re , and we’ll lay it out for you over the course of 26 episodes.”

That aspect could be a little (well, a ) navel-gazing, but there’s the outward focus the creators are bringing to the story as well, diving harshly into both the divided nature of our own real world and the coming climate apocalypse. Animation is never going to have the pace necessary to really reflect the world outside our window — it usually takes at least two years for an animated season to make it from script to screen, unless you’re South Park — but thanks to an Avatar classic (a play at a festival performed by children), we discover why the world hates the monster Korra and how the Seven Havens were formed together but now stand far apart. In the third episode, “The Order,” the airbender Karthik (Akshay Khanna) — now promoted to Commander of the Bending Brigade in Ellora — suggests they reach out to the other Havens as fewer and fewer benders are being born every year. He’s flatly turned down: Ellora can stand for itself.

This isolationist stance has been bubbling over in our real world for a long time now, and it’s hard not to watch scenes like that without thinking about Brexit or America’s increasing push to close its borders. Similarly, the threats in the first few episodes — other than a menacing red diamond; more on that in a second — are all climate based. A tornado is the “villain” of the premiere, and a massive green storm nearly destroys Ellora in Episode 2, “Into The Storm.” Again, it’s not one to one, but with our own climate disasters increasing year by year, it’s clear that DiMartino and Konietzko are setting up Seven Havens as both a commentary and a warning, while also delivering a fun mythology-building Avatar series.

Seven Havens is set up as both a commentary and a warning, while also delivering a fun mythology-building Avatar series.

Speaking of mythology-building, the first two episodes essentially function like one pilot, and are surprisingly sparse on action and plot… laudably so, as the series in those initial 40ish minutes sits in the silences and lets us feel what the characters are feeling instead of thrill at Cool Bending Fights, though there are plenty of those too. The two plot tracks follow Pavi as she rides her cat-monkey, trying to hide while a festival celebrating the rise of the Seven Havens takes over Ellora; and Jae as he works with his bending team from the town’s Bending Brigade to help fix a crumbling bridge.

Pavi is, per the title of “Book 1,” all about survival and that’s it. Jae also ties into that theme; he’s focused on protecting Ellora to a fault, though having been raised in a post-Avatar society, he doesn’t seem to understand what he’s protecting or why. When Pavi ends up accidentally causing havoc at the festival by freeing some bugs, she uses her earthbending and alerts Jae to a rogue bender. Traveling out into a storm, Jae appeals to Pavi with kindness, but they get interrupted by a tornado, which Pavi helps shut down by revealing she can also airbend. This reshapes Jae’s whole thinking: What if the Avatar a monster, but in this case a nine-year-old girl with one leg who’s just trying to live?

Jae brings her back to headquarters to try and figure out what to do, trusting his superior Karthik with the info, while Pavi sneaks off only to discover Avatar — specifically, her twin sister Nisha (Aishu Devan). Shouts to Paramount for doing a good job hiding this secret despite it being pretty obvious that front-loading twins as the main characters of the series would imply they’re the Avatar. Given what we find out shortly — that Nisha has a lot of Korra’s impulsiveness and anger in her, while Pavi has Aang’s wackiness while being all refusal no call — it’s a neat way of splitting and analyzing what made previous Avatars work (or not) thanks to the twins.

It also kicks us into our central mystery in Episode 2: Who Pavi and Nisha, why don’t they remember each other, and how are they the Avatar — the first time in the Avatar cycle that two people have held the title at the same time? Shades of Buffy and Faith on Buffy the Vampire Slayer, perhaps? Rewinding time, we get to see a little bit about how Nisha has been training in secret under the guidance of Karthik and desperately wants to go out and help. She gets her chance thanks to the aforementioned giant green storm.

While we get to see Ellora activate the Bending Brigade to mitigate the damage of the storm, which is pretty neat, the focus is on Pavi and Nisha, who eventually join together to help, only to be confronted by a strange red, pulsating diamond crackling with evil-looking energy. After it does to Karthik’s commander, who fled at the sight of it, Pavi and Nisha manage to trap it, only for the diamond to envelop them, send them to another dimension, and then hit them with what are likely missing memories. The diamond then disappears, leaving behind red crystalline structures throughout the wrecked Ellora, and again it seems pretty clear that this may not be evil so much as something reaching out — likely from the Spirit World, and potentially even an aspect of Korra; TBD on that.

This brings us to Episode 3, which thanks to an opening title sequence laying out the plot in classic Avatar style — thank goodness; it was missed in the first two half-hours — feels like the first real episode of the show. The main thrust here is that Jae is completely melting down at keeping the secret of the re-emergence of the Avatar(s), while Pavi and Nisha are at odds over doing Avatar training with the surprise return of the Order of the White Lotus, a group of wise men and women who often will help guide the Avatar. This comes together when the three characters all calm what looks like an armadillo-camel that’s been corrupted by the red energy; it acts like a pill bug rolling around Ellora, and we’ve had armadillo-bears and armadillo-tigers before.

Here we get key component of the series — the . Jeremy Zuckerman returns after working on The Last Airbender and Legend of Korra, and he’s created a heart-aching, gorgeously poignant score for the series, particularly the theme that haunts Pavi and Nisha in the first two episodes. But it isn’t until Episode 3 when Pavi plays the theme on the kalimba that it becomes clear what the real purpose of the score is. Memory is spurred on by music, and the song we’ve been hearing for two episodes so far is actually a song that Pavi and Nisha’s mother used to sing to them, complete with lyrics. It’s a goose bump-inducing moment when this is revealed, as the duo sing together on instinct, calming the animal and sparking various memories.

If there’s a criticism to be made here, it’s that it’s hard to tell exactly where this is all headed. We do get an indication when Pavi and Nisha discuss needing to go find their parents, and if this is a more emotionally driven story than the world-ending stakes facing Aang, or the threats to Republic City — and sometimes the world — that plagued Korra, it should be an interesting swerve. The show already tugs at your heartstrings from the opening moments, so this viewer at least is invested in seeing Pavi and Nisha find happiness.

Maybe as our own world has gotten murkier and more confusing, the world of Avatar has as well.

But we’re also three episodes in and have thus far encountered one (1) Haven, and even with the show just starting, you can feel time ticking away. It’s also laudable to deal with a climate apocalypse, but a green storm, a tornado, and a red diamond are not exactly the terrifying and complex villains this franchise is known for. Perhaps that’s coming: Demon-masked antagonists show up right at the end of the third episode, and likely will spur our three main characters to flee and explore more of the world, thus setting up our stakes. Maybe as our own world has gotten murkier and more confusing, the world of Avatar has as well. There’s no one evil bad guy you can defeat to save the world; it’s up to the next generation to fix things as best as they can.

These are minor quibbles when it feels so good to get back to this universe with new characters, new settings, dazzling animation, and soaring music. Welcome back, Avatar; yip yip.

Avatar Easter Eggs, References, and Connections

While most of the easter eggs and references in these episodes are pretty blatant, it might be helpful to lay some of them out for more casual viewers (or since it’s been, you know, well over a decade). Let’s start with the play about Korra performed by a bunch of kids in the town square of Ellora. Plays have been built in since “The Ember Island Players” debuted in The Last Airbender Season 3, showing off the adventures of the characters in the series via a ridiculous play titled “The Boy In The Iceberg.”

In Episode 2, Karthik reveals the lost history of the Avatars — everyone only knows Korra — and shows off a scroll depicting the older Aang with the dumb chin beard as seen in Legend of Korra, Avatar Kyoshi, and Avatar Roku. There are, FYI, a more Avatars than that, including some secret ones that were revealed in the Avatar Aang movie.

In Episode 3, we also get to see some pictures of previous members of the Order of the White Lotus. The beloved Iroh is right in the middle, with Jeong Jeong to his right and Pakku to his left — all three members of the Order during the time of The Last Airbender. Curiously, it’s harder to identify the waterbenders on the left and right side of the display; the woman all the way on the left could be Katara, but she doesn’t have the icon’s little hair loops. Other waterbenders known to be part of the Order include: Ayunerak, aka Mama, who appeared in The Dawn of Yangchen novel and has never been seen visually; Kavik, also from The Dawn of Yangchen, who has a very handsome picture but doesn’t look like the guy on the right otherwise; Ivalu, from — you won’t believe this — The Dawn Of Yangchen; and Aupilaarjuk, who was from Kyoshi’s era and only appeared in the Avatar Legends role-playing game. Sadly pictured on the wall of fame is crazy old Bumi, the earthbending King of Omashu.

Also of note? The entire Haven of Ellora seems to be laid out like the symbol for the Order, which certainly implies a lack of coincidence in the Avatars ending up there. That said, we have yet to see the other six Havens, so maybe they’re all laid out the same with their own divisions of the Order.

Less an easter egg than a nice, progressive note: Jae has a boyfriend named Datu (Topher Ngo). While things don’t go further than some embraces and a kiss on the cheek, this is a far cry from the surprising swerve of Korra and Asami getting together in the final seconds of Legend of Korra, a move that was lauded (yay representation!) and lambasted for its execution (the quickness and generally unclear way they “got together”). Baking in Jae and his boyfriend right in the third episode seems like a clear way to be more explicit about the inclusive world of Avatar. Similar to DiMartino and Konietzko stepping back and letting more racially appropriate voices write, direct, and act, this shows a welcome growth from where they were a decade ago; they’ve clearly been listening and learning.

Finally, let’s talk about that odd red diamond. The dark energy does seem to be some sort of conduit to, or from, the spirit world, and given that we don’t know what Korra did or how Pavi and Nisha connect to this — or why there hasn’t been an Avatar in centuries — it raises a lot of questions we’ll surely explore as the show continues. Let’s throw out a crazy idea here: What if this Korra’s fault; what if was ? This is something that was dealt with before in Legend of Korra, but there’s something about this energy that’s reminiscent of energybending, the forbidden practice that Aang used to take away Fire Lord Ozai’s bending at the conclusion of The Last Airbender. Is it possible Aang broke something there that Korra was trying to fix, rather than the other way around? This is pure speculation, but why not? We’ve got plenty of episodes to be way off about these theories.

items.title: Cupertino Season 1 Premiere Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Full spoilers follow for the season premiere of CBS'

The world is a little bit easier to take when there’s a topical drama by Robert and Michelle King on our televisions. From thorny legal battles (The Good Wife, The Good Fight) to religious conundrums (Evil), the Kings have tackled some of the more complex issues in modern life with humor, pathos, and realism. Gratefully, they’re back to help us parse the current tsunami of tech threats from pervasive AI to infringed privacy with Cupertino.

"Michael & Olivia" opens with Silicon Valley lawyers Michael Price (Mike Colter) and Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller) separately getting unceremoniously canned by their tech start-up employer, S-Talk. Michael is an equity co-founder, while Olivia is a junior lawyer one year out of law school, but getting career-dumped is today’s great equalizer. As they awkwardly commiserate on the curb and share some genuine admiration for one another’s work, Olivia throws him an information bone because he’s always been nice to her. While working with owner Richard Everett (Will Brill), she heard him asking someone how to fire an equity partner for cause while keeping their money… meaning Michael was unlawfully pushed out.

From that little moment of allegiance blooms the duo who are the beating heart of Cupertino. Colter’s been a ride-or-die actor for the Kings going back to The Good Wife, and here he brings smarts, charisma, and simmering sex appeal to Michael Price. Though this character wears tailored suits and comes from a prestigious family of lawyers, Michael is a believer in the Davids battling these tech Goliaths, which keeps him grounded and empathetic. The yin to his yang is Rachel Keller’s Olivia, who is shrewd yet green. Post law school, she migrated straight to Silicon Valley from the sheltered arms of her rural Christian family, so there’s plenty for her to navigate as she starts swimming with the sharks. Fresh from the series , Keller was also stellar in FX’s so it's exciting to see her go toe-to-toe with not only Colter but Cupertino’s ever-expanding ensemble of top-notch recurring actors to come, including Girls5eva alums Busy Philipps and Renée Elise Goldsberry, Joe Morton, and Jackie Earle Haley.

If you’re an existing fan of the Kings’ work, Cupertino feels a little like comfort television because it utilizes many of their signature storytelling elements: ripped-from-the-headline cases; the casting of theater-great character actors; storylines that breathlessly twist on a dime; and their ability to make serious subjects comprehensible, weird, and entertaining. They’ve even 2.0’d their The Good Fight lady fixer character Marissa Gold, updating her as Michael and Olivia’s Gen Z street-smart office manager, Christy Palladino (Ella Stiller).

Cupertino reminds us that there’s no shame in being a broadcast procedural when you’re working at the level of the Kings and their collaborators. 

Yet familiar doesn’t mean this is a dumbed-down procedural by any means. The Cupertino pilot alone tackles tech industry sexual harassment and equity disparity, stealing personhood for LLMs, and the fragility of tech bros with their shell games and unethical smoke screens. It’s all presented with wit and intelligence, and through characters who bring us into this alien world of stealth technology and can decipher this industry that's moving too fast and breaking things with seeming impunity. Cupertino reminds us that there’s no shame in being a broadcast procedural when you’re working at the level of the Kings and their collaborators.

If The Good Wife and The Good Fight could give me an understanding of Constitutional law and systemic governmental flaws, I can’t wait to see what the Kings school me on with Cupertino.

items.title: HBO's War: Season 1, Episode 2 Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
After a heavy dose of frenetic table-setting in , War’s second episode — sharply written by George Kay and deftly directed by Ben Taylor — slows its pacing down a bit as Morgan (Dominic West) and Carla (Sienna Miller) and their respective legal teams enter the pivotal three-day mediation period of their divorce.

Morgan and Carla are each instructed by their teams to put on amicable fronts as both sides strategize how to strike the best deal. That means a lot of strained smiles and literal hand-holding between the divorcing spouses to mask any anger and bitterness. Their facades just barely hold. Behind the scenes, their teams are reckoning how to protect their clients and gain the upper hand.

After Carla was surprised on the red carpet with divorce papers, her lawyers at Taylor & Byrne want to control the developing narrative, namely the matter of Flora Monroe (Rose Williams), the young actress Carla enlisted to honey-trap Morgan in a one night stand.

Taylor & Byrne partner Serena (Phoebe Fox) tries to convince Flora to sign an NDA as a means to protect herself and Carla, but Flora is unnerved by the request. She’s not fond of being paid off as if she were a prostitute. Flora insists she chose to sleep with Morgan because she found him attractive.

Serena’s plan ends up backfiring spectacularly because her new hire, Johnny (Archie Renaux), is secretly on his first assignment as the mole for Morgan’s lawyers at Cathcarts. Johnny is funneling information to both firms about Serena’s offer to compensate Flora and detailing the shakedown engineered by Flora’s greedy mother Mumsy (a scene-stealing Camille Coduri). Needless to say, things are getting messy and murky for everyone as both legal teams play dirty.

Then there’s the curious implication that Johnny is growing romantically (or just sexually) interested in Carla and/or Flora. He hasn’t outright said anything but his search history and longing looks don’t lie. Johnny seems poised to not only screw up his relationship with his girlfriend Bella (Honor Swinton Byrne) but the entire divorce case for both firms.

Flora also seems ready to make things even worse for herself by texting Morgan in the episode’s closing moments. Is she playing her own separate angle or does she legitimately want to be with Morgan romantically again? We shall see.

West and Miller excel in this episode at smiling through their teeth at each other, while Renaux continues to find the humanizing nuances in the double-dealing Johnny. Fox’s Serena seems like the closest thing to a good guy in this story, but there’s enough iffy moral resolve in her that maybe she will end up surprising viewers with an eventual turn to the dark side.

As Serena’s adversaries Beatrice “Queen Bea” Ubosi and St John Smallwood, respectively, Nina Sosanya and Pip Torrens continue to be a great one-two punch duo who find enough wit and aplomb in their predatory characters to put the guilty in guilty pleasure.

items.title: Other Mommy Review
items.author: CarlosAMorales
items.content:
Other Mommy is in theaters now.

Although she’s made her reputation (and her Academy Award) on prestige dramas, Jessica Chastain is no stranger to horror. The Sacramento-born thespian has starred in the likes of Mama, It: Chapter Two, and the underrated Guillermo del Toro joint Crimson Peak, and once more returns to the genre with , a new film from director Rob Savage where Chastain plays the dual role of a mother and her demonic doppelganger. Sadly, the film wastes what should be a slam dunk premise (and a trailer that based on a well-timed jump scare) on a generic script and not enough ideas to fill out even its brisk 90-minute runtime.

Arabella Olivia Clark stars as Bela, a seven-year-old girl living a not-quite idyllic suburban family life with distant mother Ursula (Chastain) and doting father Russell (Jay Duplass). There’s some tension in the home stemming from Ursula’s seeming workaholic lifestyle that Bela is already aware is actually a cover for her mother having an affair, but not enough that her parents haven’t been blissfully unaware that Bela has been hanging out with a not-imaginary friend named Other Mommy (also Chastain). Other Mommy loves spending time with Bela when Ursula can’t be bothered but also won’t stop insisting that Bela agree to let Other Mommy “into her heart,” the outcome of which is assuredly some form of demonic possession but also isn’t explained enough for the audience to dread it.

What follows is a surprisingly quick acknowledgment from Ursula and Russell that something supernatural is going on, and the family fleeing their home to locale after locale where Other Mommy inevitably arrives to cause more mystic mayhem. In a strange move for a movie like this, Savage rarely tries to mine fear from the setting or its corruption thereof, instead betting all his chips on how Other Mommy distorts herself and the scene around her with reality-warping powers that can’t help but come off like hollow, budget-conscious spectacle. The inconsistency in how Other Mommy’s sinister illusions manifest removes a lot of their bite; one scene features an extended shot of Chastain’s neck stretching with unconvincing CGI, while another features some agreeably gooey practical body horror that’s shown for only a few seconds. This approach results in a movie that doesn’t come close to being as unnerving as it clearly wants to be.

Other Mommy can't settle on a coherent identity, instead grabbing bits and pieces of other movies and trying them on for size.

Not helping matters is the impression that the movie can’t settle on a coherent identity, instead grabbing bits and pieces from other movies and trying them on for size like Other Mommy does with other people’s skins. Savage invokes movies like It, Smile, Coraline, and The Conjuring (that last one is understandable given James Wan’s producer credit here), but never delivers an iconic visual or concept that other movies could hypothetically crib from him. Even the main conceit of Chastain playing the dual lead role is watered down by Other Mommy sometimes taking on different disguises, a confounding gambit given that the movie never tries to generate suspense from the characters possibly not knowing who in the room is Other Mommy. It all leads to a conclusion centered around revealing the dark family secret that made Other Mommy target Bela in the first place, but the answer is too little too late to make the journey worth the effort.

Still, the reason to see this is why anyone will bother picking up a ticket: Jessica Chastain breaking bad as Other Mommy. Chastain taking her bread and butter intensity and channeling it into a maternal Deadite is the kind of hook that will likely catapult Other Mommy to profitability regardless of critical reviews. If only Savage was more willing to trust his leading lady, often smothering Chastain’s incredible physical performance with droopy facial VFX and rapid cuts. Nathan Elston's screenplay also never gives her a character to play on the other side of the coin, with Ursula being more of a checklist of “unattentive mother” tropes instead of a human being. There’s no exploration of Ursula’s emotional reality and why she can only seem to care for Bela in an ancillary capacity to make effective contrast with Other Mommy’s malicious clinginess. If Ursula doesn’t want to be part of the family, what she want? The movie doesn’t seem to know.

Chastain still commits even with such flimsy material, and to give Savage credit, he does a great job directing Arabella Olivia Clark to a child performance that’s one of the best parts of the movie. Bela has more screen time than anyone else, and the movie avoids many of the pitfalls of having a child lead even when the storytelling often comes up short in other ways. The most specificity that the family unit gets is everyone referring to Russell as “Daddo” instead of “Daddy” – a cute detail that wouldn’t be remarkable if the movie didn’t have an emotional vacancy where its dramatic engine should be. Even the gore and scare sequences don't leave much impact beyond a couple of early exceptions, resulting in a film that unfortunately runs out of energy long before the credits roll.

items.title: Animals Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
is in select theaters and on Netflix on October 9.

Ben Affleck is back behind and in front of the camera with Animals, an entertaining new thriller that spices up the kidnap movie formula with a neat twist that asks big moral questions of its protagonists and viewers.

Affleck plays Mark Kimball, a tycoon running as an independent candidate to become the next mayor of Los Angeles. (It should be noted that LA is currently in a heated mayoral campaign, so kudos, Netflix, on the timing of your film’s release.) Mark is a middle-aged white male Army veteran with progressive views and a Black wife and mixed-race son, who takes no outside funding and speaks fluent Spanish. It’s a cynical political strategist’s dream candidate come true, something the film acknowledges.

It’s Halloween and LA is just days away from electing its next mayor. Mark has run a vigorous, self-funded campaign, and yet he’s behind enough that he could lose the election and with it, all the fortune he’s poured into it. His therapist wife Abigail (Kerry Washington) doesn’t know the extent to which he’s spent their savings on his campaign. And what Mark doesn’t know about – but which was revealed in the trailer – is that Abigail is having an affair (the other man is played by Affleck’s Justice League co-star Ray Fisher).

Mark and Abigail get a call from an unknown man who reveals that he’s kidnapped their son Denny (Christopher Woodley) and demands a $7 million ransom, money they don’t have on hand because it’s all tied up in Mark’s self-funded campaign. In their desperation, they agree to Mark’s campaign manager Sam’s (Steven Yeun) idea of bringing in mysterious fixer Dayle Burton (Gillian Anderson), who can procure the ransom money (with additional fees involved, of course). The stone-cold, all-business Dayle commences schooling Mark and Abigail on how to deal with the kidnapper while also debunking any illusions they may have about human nature and moral stances.

The film’s big twist – which I will not reveal here – spins the movie into a far more compelling direction, both plot-wise and thematically. Until that point, Animals was an engaging flick, but it wasn’t doing anything much different from what we’ve already seen in other kidnapping movies like Ransom (i.e., who can you trust, who is the kidnapper, lots of harrowing phone calls, etc). But the twist then triggers a host of moral quandaries for Mark and Abigail to wrestle with while also forcing them to confront bitter truths about each other and their relationship.

Affleck and Washington make their characters three-dimensional, flawed people. Both Mark and Abigail can be hypocritical and selfish at times, and have been unable to speak plainly about their problems with each other until this unthinkable crime happens. They hit each other with some hard truths, and the actors do a good job of capturing the strains in the marriage.

Animals takes place after the fires that devastated LA in 2025, and that palpable anger against the political establishment, and how the haves and have-nots have fared since, is a key factor in the film. While Animals reflects the city’s socioeconomic layers and diverse populace, LA is used here as a microcosm of the US for a broader thematic and political commentary about the rich and the poor and American citizens and undocumented immigrants. All said, Animals gets pretty bleak and cynical in its depiction of human nature and the price of victory.

items.title: Matchbox The Movie Review
items.author: Matt Fowler
items.content:
It's hard separating the cars from the cartist here. Matchbox The Movie starts as a ridiculous ad for the 70-year-old toy line, which are literally just small die-cast metal cars, and then cranks up its volume for some empty, fleeting nonsense. Apple TV has a strong case for having the best quality shows of the Streaming Wars but it's not perfect. Like other streamers, it's also given us dumb bullshit. Let's dig deeper...

Sadly, the best thing about Matchbox The Movie -- which is that it goes overboard with large-scale, globe-trotting action -- is hamstrung by it being a watch at home on your couch affair. Look, it's all forgettable, and a waste of a Marvel movie-sized budget, but at least on the big screen the big set pieces from director Sam Hargrave (stunt coordinator for Infinity War and Endgame, director of both Extraction* flicks for Netflix) could get the presentation everyone's hard work deserves. Nothing's ever going to take your breath away on a 55" screen though.

(*Despite them also being non-theatrical releases, y'all should check out the insane Oners in this franchise.)

Matchbox The Movie centers on middle school friends in a small Ohio town, who call themselves the Matchbox Gang (ugh) because they somehow enjoy playing with teensy cars in the year of our lord 1997. Four of them grow up to have careers based on the specific Matchbox vehicle they liked as a kid (you can almost hear the Mattel boardroom execs hubbub positively at this idea). One of the gang, however, Sean, moves away and winds up becoming a no-ties, family-doesn't-exist dickhead secret agent. John Cena plays adult Sean, who returns home after decades and inadvertently gets his estranged pals roped up in a dangerous international conspiracy involving a missing nuke. Now they all must work together to clear their names and save the day.

Jessica Biel, Teyonah Parris, Sam Richardson, and Arturo Castro round out the cast, along with Danai Gurira, and Corey Stoll. None of these folks are to blame here. They're all fun, talented performers more or less wasted in a movie that feels like it came from an episode of The Studio (also available on Apple TV). It just makes you feel bad when these guys do their best to make the movie's meager emotional moments work.

"Matchbox is glitzy, glossy and hollow, never even trying to present something original.

These aren't really characters, though, they're brief character summaries. Construction truck guy never wants to leave town. His flying wife wants to see the world. Paramedic race car woman wants to help people. And quickly. Fun fact: Since race car lady (Biel) is the woman Cena's spy dude has been pining for, she has to be available. But it's been decades so she had to have before. I thought to myself, "I bet she says I was married, ." And guess what, you guys?

Matchbox is glitzy, glossy and hollow, never even trying to present something original. Everything is safe and familiar and easy, which has always been Hollywood's go-to answer for trying to hit as many quadrants as possible, thus potentially making the most money. But it's always, no matter how many times the lesson hasn't been learned, led to unexceptional dust. You also can't trick people into thinking your movie is good by having your characters recurrently reference better action movies.

There's a chance this will be a disposable "streaming hit." Like a Red Notice or a Back in Action or a War Machine. It's a futile accolade, based on metrics with too many loopholes, workarounds, and sleight of hand. It means people will put this on their TV, on a service they already subscribe to. It could be on in the background or it could provide TV light while falling asleep. What it definitely means is that people will easily do that rather than buy a ticket to see it in the theater.

Let's talk about what this is: it's a multi-million dollar mistake based on the worst takeaways from the massive success of the Barbie movie. It was movie studio and toy company heads thinking that Barbie was a hit because it was based on doll people know. There could be no other reason, right, that people, primarily women, went and saw Barbie over and over again? Here now stands the grotesque love child of this obtuse reasoning. There were then pitches all over town for toy movies. What can we do with Matchbox? The answer is, obviously, nothing. Now, I firmly believe that this film was probably the idea for a Matchbox movie. But the best idea for a Matchbox movie is still a terrible idea for a movie. If something's the best-worst, or the least-awful, don't make it.

Ultimately, any movie based on a toy or a video game or a comic is an ad for that product. Barbie worked because it magically side-stepped that puddle by being about something socially relevant and important. Matchbox was never ever going to be capable of that. Barbie was also damn funny. This movie has laughs you can count on one hand if you're feeling charitable (all, in part, thanks to Sam Richardson). Matchbox The Movie is like when Wayne's World had to shill for Noah's Arcade. There's even a moment in the beginning where a character muses about the history of the Matchbox toy line, like it's Americana we should salute.

items.title: Fjord Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
will be released in theaters October 9.

How well do you truly know your neighbor? How much do you actually to?

These are the questions at the heart of Fjord, a fraught drama that becomes about opposing families caught on either side of a “culture war” while seeming to care rather little for the people themselves. Centering on a religious Romanian family who immigrate to a chilly remote village in Norway, where they soon find themselves coming under scrutiny by the more progressive community when suspected of abusing their children, it’s a film that feels designed to challenge the preconceptions of all who see it. But rather than succeed at doing so, it ends up painting with far too broad a brush, capturing plenty of beautiful, haunting landscapes while leaving the actual people populating them at a perpetual distance. Even with Marvel star giving one of his best, most understated performances to date alongside the always magnificent Renate Reinsve of The Worst Person in the World, there’s no shaking just how cold and alienating it all becomes the longer that it goes on.

Whether this is the ultimate goal is something worth interrogating, but it’s still a shame to see so much talent squandered on something so surprisingly shallow. Even if the point to keep us in the dark so that we’re left to reflect on our assumptions about the two perspectives at odds in the film, the results of the film’s choices still mean we’re looking down on the world from a thousand feet up in the sky. If you squint hard, you can see the complexities and contradictions being teased out by the strong cast, though this is still a strangely challenging undertaking in a film ostensibly about how people don’t care to understand each other. The frustration this creates may mirror that of the characters, but it all becomes one-note, leaving us with little to hold onto as it shifts into being a half-hearted legal thriller of sorts, as well as a look at how modern polarization can put a strain on communal living. That the film itself is then lacking in life, often reducing its characters to caricatures, is a contradiction it can’t overcome.

This is all despite the best efforts of Stan, who plays the conservative family patriarch, Mihai, and Reinsve, who plays his wife, Lisbet. Reuniting the duo after their spectacular and slept-on recent film, , the film is at its best when it just lets them authentically inhabit a scene. From the moment we first get introduced to them via a tense opening that hints at some of the truth, you almost forget that it’s Stan you’re watching. Part of this has to do with his physical appearance: Ever committed as an actor, Stan fully shaved his head. He also carries himself in a more reserved way, though it’s also the even more minute details that make you feel as if you’re just observing an awkward, overbearing father navigating his new home. Similarly, Reinsve is operating on a more reserved though no less mesmerizing wavelength, with even scenes of her just silently working genuinely drawing you in. It’s then unfortunate that, even with all this compelling work, the film increasingly pulls us further and further away from them.

For director Mungiu, who has made plenty of intriguing work in the past, such as 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days and the recent riveting R.M.N., the more low-key moments are where he’s at his best. That this gives way to a more labored, broadly-sketched series of escalations leaves little in the way of a meaningful impact. Specifically, there is a serious allegation made, and the children of the newcomers are subsequently taken by CPS. We only briefly get to know said children before they are all whisked away, ultimately preventing us from understanding what their thoughts on the situation might be or if there’s something to be gleaned from their perspectives. Instead, Fjord becomes about a banal and uncaring bureaucracy that traps the entire community in a tense standoff while never seeming to care about the richer complexities of the characters navigating it. There are interrogation scenes, courtroom confrontations, and some critical revelations scattered throughout, though they don’t cohere into anything nearly as compelling as the film was when the actors were being given room to inhabit their characters.

Indeed, by the time it all draws to a rushed close, so much is left dangling that it almost plays as a bit of a shrug. Compared to the layered nuance and quiet intensity of Mungiu’s previous work, it’s an experience that becomes more of a letdown the more you think about it. You can’t fully dismiss it, as there remains plenty of promise, but you also can’t fully embrace it either. Perhaps the filmmaker himself was searching for some greater clarity in the chaotic culture war narrative he created from real news stories he had read, but neither he nor us end up finding much of it. There is certain to be much discussion around the film, its political perspective, and what it’s trying to say, though it’s hard to feel like it was trying to say much at all.

By the time it all draws to a rushed close, so much is left dangling that it almost plays as a bit of a shrug.

Perhaps this is Mungiu trying to take a more impartial, observational perspective that could eventually allow for some deeper ideas and emotions to come pouring out. The trouble then is that there’s genuinely little to actually observe or experience, especially as it expands outward even further from the supposed main characters. What is the truth of what happened? How did all of these people come to this point? Is there anything that could possibly provide greater insight into any of them? The film’s ambivalence toward much of the complexity of this story may be an attempt at being evenhanded, but this is all a masquerade, as the film increasingly sees Mungiu putting his hand not-so-subtly on the scales. In the end, how well do we truly know any of these characters? Even if you genuinely want to, Mungiu — surprisingly — does not.

items.title: Hellraiser: Revival Review
items.author: Tristan Ogilvie
items.content:
From the opening scene of Hellraiser: Revival, in which an intimate moment of sexual fetishism goes horribly wrong for its hero and his lover, this survival horror adventure inspired by Clive Barker’s bloodsoaked ode to BDSM makes it painfully clear that it’s not for the squeamish. So graphic is its ebb and flow between blasting gory holes and bathroom glory holes that the greatest moments of tension I felt playing it were not when I was fending off its hordes of gimp-masked cultists, but rather when I was nervously looking over my shoulder just in case my wife happened to walk in the room. However, peel back the sordid surface layer and Revival doesn’t have much meat to go along with its many buckets of blood. Heavy-handed storytelling, repeated chase sequences, and uninspired boss encounters meant that no matter how many meatsacks had their skin pierced and flayed by chains that tightened onscreen, Hellraiser: Revival never managed to properly get its hooks into me.

We play as Aiden, a one liner-spouting everyman with some troubling addiction problems who’s on a quest to bring his newly murdered girlfriend back to life the only way he knows how: by making a pact with pale-skinned series poster boy, Pinhead (voiced with trademark unnerving eloquence by original actor Doug Bradley), to slaughter several members of a local death cult and feed their hearts to her partially reanimated remains. It’s a disturbing premise that’s pretty faithful to the first (and best) two films in the Hellraiser series, but I wish its plot was presented in a more dynamic fashion. The exceedingly gory scenes that featured Pinhead and his cenobite pals always had me glued to the screen, but so much of Revival’s roughly nine-hour story is otherwise delivered in drawn-out exposition dumps spouted by secondary characters, and I never really felt too invested beyond the broad strokes. It’s not a great sign when the chatty in-game merchant is doing most of the heavy lifting here, and I’m not just talking about her ammo crates.

Still, at least the shooting is pretty solid, albeit fairly stock standard for the survival horror genre. To be honest, if Revival’s weapon and inventory system borrowed any more from the Resident Evil series you could probably squint and spot a Capcom logo watermarked somewhere onscreen. However, its assortment of upgradeable pistols, shotguns, machine guns, and breakable blades and bats facilitate some fun ways to decapitate and dismember the hedonistic hordes that stand in Aiden’s way, and ammo is scarce enough that I was forced to make use of absolutely everything at my disposal.

I admittedly had to toggle off the overzealous aim assist since it would regularly snap to a single enemy when I was trying to target an explosive barrel in the middle of a group, and I also lamented Aiden’s inability to vault over obstacles. This became particularly ludicrous in one instance where I could clearly see a room full of precious items through a wide open window, but instead of simply jumping through the gap, I had to stop and hunt around for a key to the locked door in order to access them.

If Revival’s weapon and inventory system borrowed any more from the Resident Evil series you could probably squint and spot a Capcom logo watermarked somewhere onscreen.

Even so, Revival’s mixture of slash-and-sidestep melee encounters and skull-shattering shotgun blasts makes for some gory good times, even if the variety of enemy types is somewhat limited. Beyond the machete and gun-wielding cultists, it’s mostly the same gaggle of gangly ghouls, suicide-bombing beasts, and legless creatures crawling after you that you have to mow down.

There are ample opportunities for stealth, too, with bricks and bottles to throw for distractions and violent stealth kills to pull off. Although I wish there were controls to peek around corners like in the recent Silent Hill: Townfall, because too often I’d be spotted ever-so-slightly stepping out from cover and be forced to go in all-guns-blazing anyway. It was even worse during the occasional instant-fail stealth sections with stalker enemy types, who could sometimes spot me through bushes even when I was standing still.

What elevates Revival’s combat slightly above the norm is the introduction of the Genesis Configuration, a powerful reimagining of the series’ iconic puzzle box that gives Aiden the ability to grab objects like conveniently placed nails and sawblades from his surroundings and hurl them at enemies with forceful blasts of telekinesis. Use of these BioShock-style superpowers is tied to his ‘suffering’ bar, which must be continually topped up by staggering enemies and performing a grisly execution move that jams the hellraising Rubik’s Cube into their mouths and blasts nine inch nails directly into their skulls like they’re front row at Coachella.

I like that the limitations of the suffering bar means these supernatural abilities don’t make you feel too overpowered, and how the short timer on keeping an object suspended in stasis means you can’t confidently wander around with a fanblade ready to launch like you could in Dead Space. Eventually these powers are expanded to let Aiden play with fire, which allowed me to shoot explosive barrels to take out one group of enemies, before hoovering up the resulting flames and hurling them at other monsters hustling over to provide backup. There’s even a bar-draining super move that shackles clusters of creatures together and tears them all apart at the same time, chaining your attacks in a gruesomely literal sense. It’s just a shame that this devastating option for crowd control doesn’t arrive until much later in the story, giving you relatively few opportunities to really put it to use.

It’s also disappointing that Revival’s boss fights are so utterly flat and forgettable for the most part. There are some interesting exceptions like the flying Sister of Mercy, who shrouds the arena in a blood mist and darts at you through the crimson haze, and another beast that scrambles on all fours and locks you in a cage suspended from a tree branch, forcing you to desperately fend off ghouls clumsily climbing up the bars in order to escape and finish the fight. But too many of the boss encounters are boring, close-quarters clashes that barely raise a hair let alone hell, and are just not all that engaging to overcome.

A skinless freak that sluices down into a pool of viscera like some sort of blood-splattered Splatoon character certainly makes one hell of an entrance, but the fight itself demands little in the way of strategy beyond circle-strafing and shooting him until he’s done for. Ditto the second time you face him later on. Meanwhile a sluglike cenobite that has enough arms to give himself a group hug is equally one-note, and you have to fight him a staggering total of over the full course of the journey. For all the sharp objects that litter its environments, it's somewhat surprising that Revival’s boss fights can frequently be so dull.

For all the sharp objects that litter its environments, it's somewhat surprising that Revival’s boss fights can frequently be so dull.

Revival’s puzzles aren’t the sharpest either, typically limited to tried and tested tasks like searching for bolt cutters to bust open chained gates or scouring documents for clues to four-digit keypads. There are at least a handful of occasions where it really leans into its seedier – and at times sillier – side with quandaries that are designed to tease not just your brain but potentially other parts of your anatomy. (No judgement.) At one point I was asked by a latex-clad NPC to go on a treasure hunt for uncomfortable-looking toys in a bondage club in order to progress the story, while at another I found myself flummoxed by a combination lock that demanded I arrange the positions of a variety of couples in an orgy. Truly there are moments where Revival feels a bit like Resident Evil if you swapped out Leon Kennedy for Leisure Suit Larry, and while none of its puzzles are particularly challenging, a number of them are at the very least somewhat unique.

Yet while Revival might be sexually depraved, it’s also disappointingly deprived of any interesting new gameplay ideas elsewhere, regularly cribbing from survival horror classics without doing enough to match them, let alone improve on them. Remember the frantic cabin defense in Resident Evil 4 that saw Leon team up with Luis to board up windows and kick down ladders as crazed villagers spilled in through every entry point? Well, there’s a version of that here set in a much smaller, single-storey space that inspires considerably less in the way of panicked problem solving. How about a looping household hallway a la Hideo Kojima’s P.T.? Yep, that’s in here too, minus any interesting puzzle elements or baby-in-the-sink levels of genuine terror.

Even the absolute fundamentals are regularly fumbled. At one point I powered up an old elevator, and as I waited for it to make its agonisingly slow ascent to my level I steeled myself for a fight, since as we all know nothing spawns enemies faster in a survival horror game than the simple press of a call button. However, as the gun-toting goons inevitably started filing into the room from all corners, I discovered that I could just leave the building through the front door and gun them all down while they funnelled their way through the exit, which completely robbed the moment of its intended intensity.

In occasional departures from the slaughter-filled hallways of sex clubs and cult leader mansions, Aiden is regularly whisked away to the Labyrinth for a brief break from combat. Although this MC Escher-inspired maze of concrete corridors is far more linear than it initially appears, it nonetheless does a great job of capturing the ominous feel of Hellraiser’s infamous realm of torture and pain. From the looming Leviathan on the hellscape’s horizon to the insect-like cenobites that scatter along the walls like grotesquely fleshy cockroaches, it’s initially a very intimidating place to explore. Every jagged surface looks like it could have your eye out, and Revival plays some clever tricks on you to keep you on your toes, like rearranging the walls around you to make you feel like you’re really trapped inside a tangle of impossible architecture.

[Revival] does a great job of capturing the ominous feel of Hellraiser’s infamous realm of torture and pain.

I very much enjoyed the occasional use of Aiden’s telekinesis power to manipulate large chunks of the environment and create paths through this otherworld, as well as dashing past its spinning instant-deathtraps in order to snare optional upgrades to Aiden’s health and suffering bars. What I did grow tired of, though, were the overused chase sequences that see you pursued by Chatterer, the cenobite from the films that basically resembles a wind-up pair of chattering teeth being smuggled inside a stretched-out skinsuit. The first instance of me being hunted by this rictus-grinning goon certainly may have gotten my blood pumping, but by the third of fourth instance of sliding under the same clusters of chains and obstacles, my heart rate had dipped well below the speed of his perpetually pattering pearly whites.

Still, even though my repeat runs through Revival’s mazes eventually became monotonous, at least they consistently functioned as intended. Back in the story’s mortal realm, things didn’t always seem to go to plan. Beyond minor bugs like enemies glitching through walls and audio dropping out during boss fights that made them seem more silent than violent, there were a handful of more significant errors in the PS5 version I played that, while never completely gamebreaking, were pretty annoying to endure. In one instance, I’d fought my way to a cabin deep in a cemetery and puzzled open a locked safe, only to find that I had no inventory space to claim the gun upgrade inside it. So, I trudged all the way back to the nearest save point to temporarily offload some weapons and ammo into a storage box, only to return to the safe and be frustrated to find it locked again with no button prompt to reopen it.

Later on, I was surprised to find the door to a safehouse had somehow become stuck and wouldn’t budge. It was open wide enough to let me see the merchant calmly blinking back at me, but I couldn’t get close enough to actually buy anything from her. This meant that for about a 30-minute stretch at the more combat-heavy end of the story, I was forced to make do with the scarce amount of ammo I could scrounge from the environment until I finally battled through a number of enemies and a boss fight on my way to the next save point, which made that period substantially more of a grind than it probably should have been.

However, at least I’ll only ever have to suffer these problems once, because although Revival cribs plenty from other, better survival horror series’ like Resident Evil and Silent Hill, one thing it hasn’t replicated is their signature replayability. Although there are two endings to achieve, they each stem from the one binary decision made at the story’s climax, meaning I was able to instantly reload my last save and experience both without having to play through the full story a second time. No matter whether you opt for the thoroughly bleak or more optimistic of the two outcomes, this tale eventually closes with a Pinhead quote that reads, “Your suffering has only just begun, we have such sights to show you.” Apparently those sights don’t include a New Game+ mode or any other form of unlockables, though, because Revival simply boots you out to the main menu with nothing extra to reward you with for completing its story.

items.title: Below Review
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
is now streaming on Netflix.

Set in a tiny, remote coastal town that’s suddenly facing a mysterious threat from the sea, Netflix’s new drama/horror series Below is in the unfortunate position of being compared to Widow’s Bay, the other show that already did that this year. It’s a “what if Jaws but…” vehicle for Josh Hartnett, on a career upswing with things like Oppenheimer, Trap (yes, Trap), and a great episode of Black Mirror. And while he’s doing all he can here, in a thick Newfoundland accent no less, to carry the six-episode series, Below can’t keep pace with the show. A relatively solid first half of episodes is done in by the back three that messily (and occasionally ridiculously) tie up a story that hasn’t fully found its sea legs.

Hartnett stars as Calvin Penney, a man with a trauma-filled life dating back to his family’s forced resettlement from one remote town to the slightly less remote town of Snook’s Arm (which, in real life, was resettled in 2018). As seen in the opening scene from 1986, a young Calvin, his sister Ruth, his mother, father, and a resettlement officer tow the Penny family’s whole-ass house behind a tiny, puttering boat. But something terrible happens; the Penny’s house is pulled under water and Calvin’s father, Leo, goes down with it, and Calvin cuts the line from the house to the boat to save the rest of his family. During this accident, Calvin sees — a cliché that isn’t just used as marketing for Below, but is repeated several times throughout the series — that looks like a void. Or rather, the gigantic eye of a very large beast that lives in these waters.

Fast forward 40 years and a Hartnett-aged Calvin is still living in Snook’s Arm, now a widow, hauling pieces of flaked-off iceberg back to the docks to sell to make into iceberg vodka (also a real thing). A family called the Crockers owns the distillery, owns Calvin’s boat, and has investments in seemingly every darned thing in sight, including the nearby Ocean Science Center where lead researcher Dr. Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis) studies marine samples and odd wildlife occurrences, like a flamingo landing on a resident’s roof. If you haven’t already guessed it, Below is about climate change and capitalism and what we’ve lost and what we can still preserve now that both of these things have become an insidious part of life. It’s just that Below doesn’t offer much more insight into these themes beyond broadly gesturing to the landscape and saying, with gumption, “.”

It’s a shame its thesis is so shallow because it really does begin with a promising hook: A massive chunk of iceberg floats into Snook’s Arm harbor, but the ice from it, which could be a cash cow for the local ice harvesters, oddly isn’t right. At the same time, animals and people start mysteriously dying when they’re near the water (don’t forget, something’s in it!), and the first episode ends on a shocking image I won’t spoil. What is distinctly interesting about Below is that it lets you think the provenance of all the suspicious goings-on could be anything, real or mystical, before revealing that, actually, they can all be explained with science — marine zoobiology, to be specific — or, of course, the avarice of capitalism.

Below takes place during a Come Home Year, wherein residents and family who have scattered return for festivities and local traditions like kissing fish in Snook’s Arm’s one and only dive bar. Calvin has his mushroom-addled son, Wade (Charlie Heaton), still living with him at home — Hartnett and Heaton’s scenes together are some of the strongest in Below — but his other two 20-something kids who left the roost, Mary (Ruby Stokes) and Jay (Rohan Campbell), come back too, each with their own cosmopolitan issues.

Mary has a boyfriend she desperately wants her dad to like and Jay seems to be in some shit, getting texted threats like, “Your [sic] a dead man.” (Typos, very scary.) As the season wears on, the Penny family bench catches a severe case of too much and not enough, where nearly everyone’s arc could have used a lot more attention with a couple more episodes.

Below takes an especially wild turn in Episode 4 — that includes a deep-water scene that I kind of can’t believe exists in the context of some other not-so-distant real-life events — and everything that follows plays out as rushed attempts to provide answers to the series’ questions. There are some answers, sure, but they aren’t particularly satisfying. And it’s still full of holes, enough to sink a boat.

items.title: Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
The first Dark Arisen expansion for the original Dragon’s Dogma has a well-lauded place in video game history as the expansion that “fixed” the base game, sanding down the rough technical edges and tweaking things to make the notoriously obtuse RPG more approachable. It also added hours of new content, spiraling an already heady story directly into the heavens on the back of dragon wings. Dark Arisen 2 isn’t as transformational as the first one was, primarily because many of Dragon’s Dogma 2’s biggest issues have been fixed through incremental patching since it came out in 2024. But the new content here definitely flies in the same ambitious skies as its predecessor, pushing the story and world design to new heights, even if some of the new progression options get left behind.

As with Dragon’s Dogma 2’s base campaign, Dark Arisen 2’s story remixes themes from the first game without being a simple retelling. Like in the first, another Arisen has been rumored to exist, something that shouldn’t be possible and demands your immediate attention. This takes you north to the frozen mountains of Norgan, a place that is largely abandoned save for the single settlement at its border (and the steady stream of visitors coming from other lands to investigate what’s been lost under all that ice besides you).

The expansion’s story also meanders in similar ways to the base game, with plot points getting sidetracked by little tasks or other happenings, but it didn’t feel as distracting since a lot of the “help me and I’ll help you” quests are relegated to side stories. As a whole, this roughly 20-hour main quest is solid, lacking in nuanced writing or ground breaking storytelling but bursting with a tangibly broody mood, big moments, and some genuinely interesting lore. It’s meditation on how a hero of destiny chooses their fate (if they get a choice at all) is unsubtle, and spends far too long at the end really sending the message home, but it sticks it.

For those who don’t mind a lot of filler with their killer, there are plenty of people with tasks thoroughly less vital to the survival of reality that need doing. A couple of those quest lines stand out – one where you help the son of the village’s leader become brave and tough enough to follow in his footsteps, for example – but most are just a flimsy excuse to run around the world and beat up enemies.

The frigid Norgan region is delightfully dense with things to find and see even if its smaller than most other regions in Dragon’s Dogma 2. What it lacks in square footage on a map, it gains in a sprawling sense of height that stretches from it’s jagged icy peaks down to winding underground caverns that spread wide and interconnect. Navigating up and down the rocks is a treacherous and daunting road at first, but climbing hooks can be used on specific poles scattered throughout to bridge elevations without the fuss.

It feels almost like a Zelda or Metroid game in ways this series never has before.

Combined with how dungeons and caves tended to loop back on themselves, revealing exits or opening doors that served as their own shortcuts into and out of zones, and Dark Arisen 2 felt almost like a Zelda or Metroid game in ways this series never has before. The abundance of portcrystals scattered around the map is another navigational relief. There are more in Norgan than there are in Vermund and Bathall combined, making travelling to different zones far more reasonable than it was in the base game.

Note that reasonable doesn’t necessarily mean easier. The portcrystal’s abundance is a practical matter, as ox carts wouldn’t last long in the harsh environments. Norgan’s wintry winds often pick up, turning snowfall into blinding whiteouts that threaten to freeze you to death if you aren’t protected by special winterized gear or new consumables designed to stave off these frost effects for a limited time. These came in abundance pretty regularly so I never felt like my life was in danger out there, but the scrambling effect it has on the minimap and how generally hard it is to see or navigate in real time made them a threat worth waiting out at camp.

Norgan’s crumbling castles and snowcapped cliffs are a welcome change of pace from the rolling hills and dense hinterlands of Vermund and he craggy deserts of Bathall. It’s also not all snowy wastes. I was surprised to see a break in the snow drifts when I came across a festering poisonous swamp. It matches thematically in that everything in it is dead (or maybe wishes it was), but areas like that and the crystal caves deep below the mountains subverted my expectations for the region in a welcome way.

The bulk of what you’ll find hidden in the snow are Spoils, a new gear type that appears in generic shapes (long weapon, aegis, etc.) at first, but is revealed to be a usable piece of equipment when appraised by one of the new NPCs. Rolling the dice for new gear was not particularly exciting, and it further isolated me from having any real attachment to my equipment in a game that already had an abundance of junk to constantly ignore. There are at least things outside of raw stats to consider, as each piece of gear can potentially have special attributes that grant passive abilities or enhance specific weapon skills – but no single piece of gear stayed in rotation long enough to be something I relied on much, with the deluge of experience points I received strapping a rocket to my leveling almost immediately.
