We get that all-important Hal/John banter back, but with the twist that comes from having a slightly younger and less mean-spirited version of Hal in the mix. It's endlessly entertaining to watch the two interact and for the Halogram to convey some of the things his flesh-and-blood self could never admit.

We're also treated to a terrific scene involving Sheriff Kerry (Kelly Macdonald) reuniting with "Hal," one that features arguably Macdonald's strongest performance in the series to date. I'm not prepared to discount the theory that she was Hal's killer just yet (particularly if it somehow involved her protecting her son), but her grief is clearly genuine regardless.

"The Jordan Boys Legacy" does share one flaw with Episode 6. The drama involving the other Rushville locals just isn't that compelling. Granted, this episode doesn't suffer nearly as much in that regard because it's so much more focused on Hal and John's investigation, but there are still a few scenes focused on these less compelling subplots. I really can't bring myself to care about the blackmail conflict between John and Maggie (Hannah Christine Shetler). So he's out $315,000 and a fancy Richard Mille watch. Why does any of that matter in the grander scheme of John's Green Lantern origin story?

It's also tough to know what to make of the Noah (Shea Pritchard) of it all. On the surface, his little Hat Day runaround isn't that compelling, either. But there's obviously something deeper at work with the character. I fully suspect we'll learn in the finale that he's some sort of human/Manhunter hybrid and is at the heart of Hal's murder (assuming Hal is even dead, which we really can't). I'm just glad the series is running out of room to prolong that particular mystery.

Finally, Episode 7 ends with John stepping foot onto an alien world for the first time. We quickly discover that Hal bequeathed a portal to Antaan's (Paul Ben-Victor) home planet, offering a glimpse of the devastation Manhunters can wreak. It's a nice change of pace seeing a setting other than Earth, even if the flat, featureless desert doesn't make for the most memorable view. It's more Stephanie Economou's eerie, discordant score that makes this setting feel hostile and otherwordly.

After a tense fear gas sequence and some more heart-to-heart moments between Hal and John, we're treated to a proper payoff to the entire sequence with the long-overdue return of Ulrich Thomsen's Sinestro. Naturally, him being marooned on a dead world instead of locked away on Oa raises more questions than it answers, but it's enough simply to see the character again. I just hope Episode 8 has enough room to address these many lingering questions and still wrap up John's season-long arc in a satisfying way. There's still a lot of ground left to cover.

items.title: Godzilla Minus Zero Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
This review is based on a screening timed to the New York Film Festival. opens in theaters in Japan on November 3 and in North America on November 6.

Godzilla movies have long had a problem: What do you do after the initial thrill of a quote/unquote Godzilla origin story? Can the filmmakers somehow continue the deep thematic underpinnings of that first adventure, even while upping the visual ante with more giant monster action? How do you offer a probing commentary about the world we live in – which is what the best of the genre is known for – when you’ve got skyscraper-sized lizards slugging it out MMA-style?

It is under these circumstances – or should I say restrictions? – that Godzilla Minus Zero enters the ring. As the sequel to the much-praised from three years ago – a picture that dealt with, among other things, notions of survivor’s guilt, hope in the face of hopelessness, found family, and more – Minus Zero is on the ropes from the start. Can returning writer-director Takashi Yamazaki wring even more out of his characters, who have already been to hell and back, while also blowin’ up stuff real good? In a word, no.

The film takes place two years after the events of Minus One, with Ryunosuke Kamiki back as Kōichi Shikishima and Minami Hamabe returning as Noriko. Kōichi, as fans of the Oscar-winning previous movie (for Best Visual Effects) will remember, is the former would-be kamikaze pilot from World War II who was instrumental in defeating Godzilla the first time around. Now married to Noriko, the woman he took in after the American air raids on Tokyo, the pair have also adopted Akiko, the orphaned baby they had cared for after that same disaster. Living happily together as a family, there’s only one thing that can ruin this idyllic picture… well, two things, since not only is Godzilla of course back, but there’s a new monster on the scene as well.

Minus Zero opens with a sequence of devastation, as this new critter lays waste to countless helpless civilians as they flee in the streets, avoiding both falling rubble from the buildings crumbling around them and lightning breath from the creature’s mouth. Yes, as fans have already figured out and as the marketing for the film has teased, this is Ghidorah, also known as King Ghidorah in the larger Toho mythology, and generally the archnemesis of the big guy for whom we have all gathered once again. (Ghidorah has also been referred to as “Monster Zero,” which helps to explain this film’s title.)

The scenes of destruction and terror are breathtaking.

These scenes of destruction and terror are breathtaking, with Yamazaki and his team of visual effects maestros once again managing to keep their creatures from feeling like CGI monstrosities. No, rather, Ghidorah, and Godzilla when he eventually shows up too, just appear to be monstrosities – humongous, slow-moving, reptile-like, and all-the more terrifying for it. Ghidorah also distinguishes himself from his counterpart with his scary yet herky-jerky, almost cat-like mannerisms.

So as soon as that first-round bell rings, the movie has already proven its VFX bona fides – to no one’s surprise. But it has also confirmed that a Godzilla Part 2 inevitably means more monsters. And look, none of this is to say that there’s anything wrong with a movie where Godzilla has to rip his own arm off because his foe’s teeth are sunk so tightly into it. We all love monster-on-monster action, but there’s no denying that the more of a mash a monster movie becomes – be it of the Toho, Universal, Alien/Xenomorph, or whatever else variety – the more it loses its edge as the human characters and their emotional baggage run the risk of looking puny in the face of these god-like creatures.

Remember what Bogart said in Casablanca? “It doesn't take much to see that the problems of three little people don't amount to a hill of beans in this crazy world.” Yes, I’m quoting Humphrey Bogart in a Godzilla review, but if there’s an issue with Minus Zero, it’s that the travails of Kōichi, Noriko, and little Akiko just pale when considering the scope of destruction that Godzilla and company are capable of. Whereas the first film framed that destruction through the lens of the trio’s trauma, not just in regards to the giant monster but also specifically around what they went through in the war, that resonance is missing here.

In fact, the most interesting character in Minus Zero is perhaps the most under-served. Kanji Murakami, played by Min Tanaka, is a scientist whose work is key to battling the monsters this time around. He’s also kind of warped, with Tanaka getting one scene in particular that is a bit too spoilery to describe here, but is also a highlight of the film. As with Kōichi and Noriko, and indeed every character in the film, the war irrevocably changed his life, and the scientist is still struggling to cope with that reality while he works to prevent a pair of living A-bombs from doing even more damage to humankind.

Speaking of which, a much ballyhooed sequence first glimpsed in the trailer last spring involving Godzilla and the Statue of Liberty is certainly something to behold here. Toho has asked critics to not reveal the specifics of this particular scene in reviews, but suffice to say that it is both everything you’ve imagined and theorized about, and at the same time none of that at all. It does connect back to Tanaka’s character in one of his darkest moments, and as a result is one of the film’s most memorable incidents of Godzilla-on-human action.

But that brings me back once again to the feeling that kept bubbling up for me while watching Godzilla Minus Zero. Even as Godzilla sets upon what looks like Spider-Noir’s version of New York City, the whole emotional underpinning of the scene is tied to Tanaka’s Murakami. Unfortunately, the character’s true motivations and how they’re ultimately resolved in the film play as more of an after-thought than Minus Zero’s thematic or emotional core, and for that film suffers.

If there is a central theme at work here, it’s the idea that no matter how hard we as a species try, we can’t outrun our own mistakes – and we’re gonna keep making them over and over again, despite the efforts of the best among us. Minus One ended with a hint of what was next for Noriko; while she miraculously survived a Godzilla attack, she also now bore a mysterious scar on her neck from the experience. It’s no surprise to learn in Minus Zero that it was no mere scar, and that in fact Noriko is now also a very important player in the fight against the monsters. But she, like Kōichi, is also a pawn in a greater game that’s happening on the world stage involving the monsters. The regular folks on the ground are the ones bearing the trauma of the battles that have been fought, but the powers that be don’t seem to care…

By the final act, you know where this is all going, and that’s fine. Monsters must brawl, and as with Minus One, the period setting of this film really adds to the luster of the visual effects and action scenes. Seeing Kōichi back in the pilot seat, this time of 1949-era fighter planes, is thrilling, and the various schemes concocted by the returning Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), now the head of the “Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau,” are often ingenious and satisfyingly crunchy in their attempts to slow down and ultimately stop Godzilla and his enemy.

items.title: Unabomber Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Unabomber covers the formative years and later arrest of Ted Kaczynski, the titular mail bomber who terrorized the US from the late 1970s until the mid-1990s. Director Janus Metz’s mixed bag of a film aims to understand the origin of a domestic terrorist but it never quite convinces or connects.

As FBI Agent Joanne Miller, Shailene Woodley — decent in a two-dimensional role almost any actress could have played — leads the surprisingly inert 1990s portions of the film chronicling the manhunt for Kaczynski, then a hermit living in the woods of Montana.

This storyline strives for serial killer movie suspense, but it never musters enough thrills to overcome its inherent tropes. It reduces the FBI’s capture of Kaczynski to a dull TV cop procedural instead of capturing the magnitude of what was a historic win for law enforcement.

What sets Unabomber apart from other projects about this notorious criminal are the portions set at Harvard University during the Cold War. This is where teenage Theodore Kaczynski (Jacob Tremblay), a brilliant mathematics student who yearns to be a philosopher, participates in a harrowing psychological experiment overseen by Professor Henry Murray (Russell Crowe).

Murray’s (now clearly unethical) program was meant to stress-test a person’s philosophical arguments, but instead it became an abusive quest to break a person until they changed. (It’s all very .)

The movie suggests that Murray ultimately unleashed a monster within Kaczynski who would later target the industrial and academic institutions he blamed for ruining the natural world and robbing humans of liberty. The reality is more complicated.

As the prodigy-era Kaczynski, Tremblay, try as he might, struggles to convey the psychological layers of his damaged character. Crowe delivers a fine but rote turn as the doctor who manipulated his student.

Murray’s actions certainly make him the heavy of this film, but Crowe plays him with enough haughtiness to prevent the character from being a complete mad scientist cliché. Like Kaczynski, Murray wants the world to know how brilliant he is but he may, in fact, just be a big loser.

If you’re on Netflix looking for something worth your while about this subject the better choice to stream would be the 2020 documentary Unabomber: In His Own Words.

items.title: We Build LEGO Mayor Manor: A Spooky, Not-So-Scary Halloween Build
items.author: Chris Reed
items.content:
The Mayor Manor, out now, is the theme's debut set (see it at Amazon). It's an engaging, enjoyable build, with a cool visual motif for LEGO to elaborate upon in the years to come.

The Mayor Manor is not ; it is open in the back like a classic dollhouse, allowing the builder to observe and stage the interior to his or her liking. It comes in nine bags – paper rather than plastic, thanks to LEGO's ongoing sustainability initiative. The switchover has been gradual, starting in 2020 and ramping up considerably in the last two years or so.

[A note about the paper bags: Make sure you shake and flatten them out completely before discarding them. Paper is not as slippery as plastic (nor as see-thru), and so if you're missing a piece, it might be stuck in the scraps. It happened to me twice during this build.]

The design is very '90s Tim-Burton-meets-Addams-Family. You have traditional spires mixed with stained glass windows, along with a foreboding gargoyle perched on the roof. The tree leaves are off-color blue and green, which creates the impression that you're viewing this house in the twilight rather than the bright light of day.

The house interior is well-appointed, featuring a fireplace which functionally connects to the house chimney on the exterior – a nice bit of logical, functional coherency. On the second floor, there's a grandfather clock with a golden pendulum and a face stuck at midnight. There's also a bookshelf, with the books inserted at various depths, which gives the space a bit of quirk and whimsy. If you enjoy putting together little builds, which you then insert, as furniture or other knick-knacks, into a larger build to create a whole? Then you'll really enjoy what's going on here.

The designers draw a clear line of distinction between the of the house, versus the house . The house has structural integrity; it's a two-story, traditionally built structure with defined rooms, level floors, and straight lines. But the facade of the house – the way it presents itself externally – is skewed, as if it's actively falling apart. LEGO accomplishes this by clipping crooked walls and roofs onto the underlying building. It's a convincing visual effect that'll make you do a double take.

Because half of the house appears destroyed and half appears relatively intact, we can imagine, in our mind's eye, how the house once appeared when it was whole. And it's especially cool to contrast that to the ruined state of the house, and see how this jagged split in the wall over here matches – like a high-concept jigsaw puzzle – to the broken wall over there.

Have you ever seen Ripley's Believe it or Not! museums in tourist areas? They're these self-billed "Odditoriums" that capitalize, P.T. Barnum style, on the off-beat and strange: "Come see a real shrunken head!" "Gaze upon an Iron Maiden torture device from medieval times!" "Young lady, have you ever laid eyes on a two-headed goat?"

I used to love these museums growing up, and I especially loved looking at their optical illusion facades from streetview, which made them appear as if they were sinking into the ground or experiencing the aftershocks of an earthquake. The closer I walked, the less convincing the illusion. But that also taught me something about myself – that knowing the 'trick' behind these illusions deepened my love for them rather than diminishing it.

I thought about this while putting together the Mayor Manor, particularly its East Wing. LEGO tells a story through its presentation; a stubborn intrusive tree has grown into the house's foundations, and over time, it's punctured through the walls and wrapped itself around half of the second floor. It implies that the house is very, very old, but also that the inhabitants of the house – the pale-faced matron with the fur-lined shawl, and the maid and butler who wait upon her – are either indifferent to what's happening or are unable to prevent it.

Are they ghosts or the undead? Were they once inhabitants of this house when they were alive? How long have they roamed these hallways in the years since? They don't look unhappy, strictly speaking.

This sort of imaginative "what-if?" roleplay is essential, I think, to your full enjoyment of adult-geared sets like these. Because unlike many other 18+ sets, this is not a painstaking replica or a pop culture artifact; this is a playset, with the dimensions and features of one. Children have the ability to construct elaborate play scenarios—a skill we often lose as we grow older. LEGO sets like these give adults tacit permission to indulge in those joys once more.

Children have the ability to construct elaborate play scenarios—a skill we often lose as we grow older.

But even if you don't have the suspension of disbelief to throw yourself into fantasy entirely, there is still childish joy and escapism in imagining the inner lives of these minifigures, and in staging dramatic scenarios when putting them out for display.
