items.title: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas – The Legacy Review
items.author: Luke Reilly
items.content:
I’m taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t come with any new IGN score, but they will re-examine what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release. By the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly rank in my long-term love for this series.

Today it’s time to go home to Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas.

Whether you remember it or not – or were too preoccupied being spoon-fed puréed fruit from a jar at the time – it’s impossible to understate what a banner year 2004 was for now-legendary video games. Just look at the line up. World of Warcraft. Half-Life 2 and Halo 2. Burnout 3 and Metal Gear Solid 3. Gran Turismo 4 and more – much more. I could absolutely go on. To emerge as the bestselling game of what may well be the greatest year we’ve ever had – in an era where it felt like the rulebook was being torn up and rewritten every other month – you had to be remarkable. You had to be rich, surprising, innovative, and essential. Simply put, to be the bestselling game of 2004, you needed to be more than great. You needed to be Grand.

While GTA III defined the fundamentals of 3D open-world design, and Vice City layered that sandbox with vibrant ’80s style and a big dose of yacht rock and yayo, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas pushed the formula to the very limits of what was actually possible on the world’s then-favourite DVD player. Despite shipping just two years after Vice City, San Andreas expanded Rockstar’s formula exponentially by introducing full-scale cities – all housed in what amounted to an entire fictional US state: the titular San Andreas. Best of all, it was still retro-tinged, set in 1992. A slightly less dramatic leap into the past than Vice City but, as someone whose adolescence was forged in the ’90s, an awesome period to revisit.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas pushed the formula to the very limits of what was actually possible on the world’s then-favourite DVD player.

At the time, it was a mindblowing achievement. The state itself covers an area roughly six times larger than Vice City. Its three major metropolises – Los Santos, San Fierro, and Las Venturas – each have their own unique visual identity. Los Santos is draped in smog, giving the whole cityscape a distinct orange haze at certain times of day. On the hottest days, a shimmering heat rises from the asphalt – a fabulously effective flourish that gives the city a truly tangible sense of temperature. San Fierro, defined by its severe hills and stretches of tramline, features an entirely different sort of climate. It’s more akin to GTA III’s Liberty City, where the tall, dense skyscrapers of the CBD create quite a bit of shade below. Las Venturas, San Andreas’ gambling haven, is dry, flat, and is at its best at neon-lit night. Each city is connected by open stretches of rolling fields, redwood forests, and rocky desert. There’s even a selection of tiny towns, farms, and factories between the major hubs.

However, while the size of the map was one thing – the fact that you can travel all over it and move from one major city to another without a single loading screen is something else altogether. Coming from Vice City, where you couldn’t cross from one island to the other without being briefly stalled by a loading screen, it was a genuinely amazing advancement. Rockstar had concocted a way to constantly stream in the world immediately around us in real-time. For its debut on PS2 – the platform that accounted for more than 17 million of San Andreas’ 27.5 million sales – this meant a neverending juggling act with the system’s limited 32MB of RAM and a relentless assault on its disc drive. You probably could’ve forgiven the Rockstar North team for adding a high-speed fighter jet to a game perpetually pulling data from its dual-layer DVD in a non-stop race against time to rapidly build the world in front of you before you reached it.

It’s arguable San Andreas’ greatest victory isn’t simply the immense geographical scale it boasted for its era. Rather, it’s the remarkable density of its various systems, ideas, and side activities.

I played an aggressive amount of San Andreas back in the mid 2000s. I tortured my PS2 until it started making weird noises, then I borrowed my sister’s and tortured it, too. Perhaps the ultimate testament to how supremely stuffed San Andreas is with things to do is just how many side modes I’ve encountered over the last week of playing that had honestly slipped my mind over the last 20 years. The valet activity? Forgot that. Trucking missions? Forgot those. Duelling lowriders? Oh, yeah! It’s like putting on an old pair of trousers and finding $20 notes in every pocket.

San Andreas almost never stops giving.

San Andreas almost never stops giving. Take its vehicles, for instance. Not only do they all handle with a genuine sense of heft that puts most GTA clones to shame – seriously, just watch as they subtly wiggle on their springs if you jerk them to a sudden halt – but there are also around 200 of them. From the minute it puts you on a bicycle, new vehicles are in virtually constant supply. Combine harvesters. Quad bikes. Articulated semi-trailers. Monster trucks. Functional forklifts. Hovercraft. A jump jet, a jetpack. No, not one or the other. Both. It’s like someone took a bunch of scribbled brainstorm notes and executed on every suggestion, without trimming any of them.

To be honest, there are times playing San Andreas where it almost feels like no idea was trimmed. Rob a house, go dancing, and stop at a minimart to play an arcade machine. Hit the gym, then hit the casino. Run a triathlon, and run a business. Go parachuting, unwind with some pool, and… role play as a pimp. I guess, strictly speaking, there was at least one idea that famously pulled out at the last minute: a sex minigame. It just wasn’t pulled out enough, so to speak. Ruled out so late in development it was impractical to completely remove it without jeopardising San Andreas’ vast, precarious, and otherwise interwoven code, Rockstar locked off the minigame beneath a non-interactive wrapper – keeping the camera entirely out of the room where the magic was happening. Modders discovered and re-enabled it in time for the PC version in 2005, triggering what became known as the Hot Coffee controversy.

The pearl clutching and hand wringing that followed was deeply embarrassing, even by mid 2000s standards. The US ESRB re-issued all versions of the game a commercially crippling Adults Only rating, and Australia temporarily banned it until the abandoned content was removed. It didn’t matter that it literally wasn’t even accessible for the majority of players on console – the matter had become politicised and the subject of massive media attention. The concept of two blocky PS2 characters goofily grinding against each other was apparently too much for adult gamers to bear. We would have to be content with wanton vehicular homicide and burning cops to a crisp. I’m hopeful that things would go a little differently more than two decades on, but I guess we have our own problems. These days I don’t know if I’m still killing people in video games, or if I’m only unaliving them.

The explosion of side activities is still only part of the San Andreas equation, as Rockstar also introduced a number of light RPG mechanics. This goes beyond the ability to customise leading man Carl Johnson’s appearance, via outfits, haircuts, tattoos, or munching down too many burgers. CJ also has a large number of improveable skills, and the more you do something, the better and more efficient he’ll get at it. Flying, fighting, driving, diving – you name it. Have a weapon you prefer? Use it as much as possible to level CJ up to ‘Hitman’ proficiency, where you can move and strafe while shooting, your lock-on range will extend, and (in the case of the four specific weapons) even dual wield them.

The improvements to the third-person shooter component in San Andreas are significant, with most of the clumsiness that tended to characterise GTA III and Vice City ironed out. A bulk of that is thanks to the ability to finally use the right analogue stick to control the camera at will – as opposed to the previous games, where the right stick was only used to look around in a stationary first-person camera. It’s the first GTA game to feel akin to a modern third-person shooter in this regard, which makes it a breeze to get accustomed to in 2026. You can also aim all weapons freely now, rather than just a select few – and the auto lock-on is otherwise intelligent enough to automatically prioritise and target threats rather than random civilians or, worse, your own gang members. Light stealth was even introduced, on the back of Rockstar’s own experimentation with the controversial Manhunt earlier the same year. CJ is able to crouch to reduce noise, a suppressed pistol has been added to the arsenal, and there’s a simple stealth kill you can perform on the unaware, indicated by the same raised-arm trigger used in Manhunt.

With more cities, more cars, and more depth than ever, you might have been wondering just how much more San Andreas could possibly have in store.

Well, I haven’t even touched on the radio stations yet, which are neck and neck with Vice City as the best they’ve ever been in the 30-year history of the series. It’s an impeccably curated soundtrack that’s one part perfect ’90s time capsule, and one part historical hip hop odyssey. That is, it didn’t just feature some of the most iconic rap tracks to emerge from the early ’90s, but it made sure to include stations dedicated to the entire ecosystem of complementary music hip hop found itself drawing inspiration from. Funk and soul. R&B and New Jack Swing. There’s perhaps no better example of that than the fact San Andreas didn’t make a choice between Charles Wright’s signature hit Express Yourself, or the 1988 reimaging from N.W.A. It simply included both. Eleven stations and over 150 songs is the bullet point, but there’s so much more to it than that. It’s the fact that they now air dynamically, meaning the song order changes and you won’t always hear the same slice of DJ banter introducing them.

Want more? Well, how about arguably the greatest arsenal of cheats codes ever assembled? Cheats to make the game easier. Cheats to make the game harder. Cheats to spawn all the greatest vehicles. Cheats to arm civilians with rocket launchers. Cheats to trigger a map-wide riot. Cheats to turn off the gravity!

want more? How about a same screen co-op mode that allows you to bring a friend into the world to wreak havoc alongside you. Is it slightly janky? Yes. Did that stop my friends and I from messing around with it constantly? Absolutely not.

Interestingly, about the only thing San Andreas seems to have fewer of is major Hollywood celebrities in the main roles. Following Vice City, San Andreas moved away from having a big-shot celebrity on deck to star as the lead character. Instead, CJ was capably and memorably played by an LA-based rapper named Young Maylay, with no previous acting experience. There are a number of recognisable names here as side characters, though, including James Woods, Peter Fonda, Charlie Murphy, Ice-T, Chris Penn, and the inimitable Sam Jackson as the iconically slimy Officer Frank Tenpenny. Is there a better GTA villain than Jackson’s Tenpenny? I don’t think there is.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is the single bestselling game on the most successful console in the history of the business. That’s not an accolade you can just earn by accident. Its unprecedented scope and astonishing depth were nothing short of witchcraft, and the incredible attention to detail was staggeringly impressive for something of its size. Its ability to support endless experimentation kept my friends and I busy for years, fooling around with its industry-leading list of cheats and its same-screen co-op chaos long after we’d all finished the story mode several times. Its soundtrack is the stuff of legend; so one-of-a-kind that not even Rockstar itself could quite reassemble the complete thing for subsequent re-releases. In 2004, GTA San Andreas was one of the most extraordinary games I’d ever played. In 2026, the hood done took me under all over again. Sure, the technical limitations of the mid 2000s are always obvious through a modern lens, but you can’t measure ambition in polygons – and GTA San Andreas is overflowing with it.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

items.title: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
There’s a theory that it’s impossible to make a piece of anti-war art set during a war – that, no matter what you do, the work itself inevitably becomes (or will be interpreted as) pro-war. I’m sympathetic to the argument; Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is a war story about how awesome it is to be a heroic ace pilot. It is also unapologetically anti-war and plays with complex ideas like the role of propaganda, the power of symbols, nationalism and globalism. And it extends to the way corporations influence and manipulate world events, social media and the rise of news that may or may not be real, the price and horrors of war, and what a world without borders might look like. Its story is often startlingly relevant, but when I think about my time with it, my mind returns to a single thought: Wings of Theve’s never directly stated but deeply held belief that the best thing that could happen to this world and its characters would be for the war to be over, and for none of them to ever fly a combat mission again. It marries exceptional air combat with a melodramatic but moving story, one of the year’s best soundtracks, and incredible visual design to make a war game that never lets you forget how terrible everything happening here is.

Wings of Theve takes place about ten years after Ace Combat 7, though you don’t need to be familiar with its predecessor to enjoy it. The Republic of Sotoa launches a blitzkrieg invasion of the Federation of Central Usea using the power of its air force and orbital missiles strikes known as Tonitrus Spears. The FCU capital of Theve falls. Shattered and broken, what’s left of the FCU fights a hopeless, defensive war from the deck of the Endurance, an aging aircraft carrier that, in better times, would have probably ended up as a museum. Your character, a nameless fighter pilot, is fished out of the ocean by one of the Endurance’s rescue helicopters, and you’re quickly assigned to fly second seat to Jan “Rex” Cope, the legendary Wings of Theve, the FCU’s ace of aces.

Trouble is, it’s all a lie. Cope is an exceptional pilot, but he’s never shot anyone down. His kill count is a myth, fabricated to give the people of Usea hope. As long as the Wings of Theve is in the skies, the story goes, the fight isn’t over. Cope’s job is to bring his squadron, Joker Flight, back with him. And he’s done it well. But his luck runs out when you run into Sotoan ace Shadow 22. But the Wings of Theve cannot die, so you inherit the mantle and Cope’s old callsign. You have become the name. And when legend becomes fact, print the legend and watch it go viral on social media. But it’s not enough for Joker Flight to just run anymore. They need to produce results. And as you start to shoot down enemy fighters, the lines between the legend of the Wings of Theve and reality start to blur.

It’s a compelling yarn that developer Project Aces has spun, and it unravels into an earnest story with the Joker Flight crew at its heart. You've got Baxter (callsign “Professor”) a former teacher turned pilot, mentor to the other members of Joker Flight, and your wingman; Tasha, Joker Flight’s youngest member, a generationally-talented civvie stunt pilot forced into service by the war who refuses to shoot anyone down; and Coster (callsign “Noise”), a quiet rock and roll enthusiast who manages to fly Tasha’s wing while blasting tunes over your comms. Many other supporting characters feed into the myth of the Wings of Theve whether it be your commanding XO, your Queen Flight counterparts, or the media machine spinning you up. And through it all, the legend of Cope (and his spirit) lingers.

Make no mistake, it is Wings of Theve’s characters that make this story work.

Maybe that sounds silly, but like everything else in Wings of Theve, it works surprisingly well and allows you to continue to build a connection to a character whose life and death are crucial to Wings of Theve’s world. And make no mistake, it is Wings of Theve’s characters that make this story work. They’re well-drawn, complex, interesting people elevated by genuinely excellent performances from the voice cast and your relationships with these characters drive much of Wings of Theve’s story. Whenever we sortied, I wanted to make sure I brought them home.

Ace Combat has long told its story from inside the cockpit, but Wings of Theve also puts your character on the Endurance’s deck, inside the mess with your fellow pilots and civvies who have sought refuge on the carrier, and inside hangars briefing rooms, among other places. These moments help you connect with the members of Joker Flight and the other people aboard the Endurance, but they also drive home the cost of the war, and make it feel like this world exists outside of the cockpit. You can’t really do much during them except look around and perform simple interactions, but they're home to some of Wings of Theve’s most memorable and affecting moments.

Ultimately, though, you’re a combat pilot; your place is in the air. And it’s here that Ace Combat soars (sorry), expertly weaving its story, moment-to-moment gameplay, and mission design into masterful, elegant maneuvers worthy of a state-of-the-art fighter jet. Like its predecessors, Wings of Theve is a mission-based game. After you’ve been briefed on your next sortie, you’ll select your aircraft, weapons, and parts – which you can buy (along with new planes) with points you earn by completing missions. All that affects everything from how many missiles or special weapons you can equip or how much damage they do to how well your plane handles. You can even outfit your crew’s planes if you want (or have them auto-assigned something that fits the mission at hand). Then you’re airborne, and it’s time to fly.

Often, things start pretty simply. Maybe you need to defend the Endurance, assault an air field, protect a friendly plane, or take out some transports. But these initial objectives are just a reason to take to the air. The beauty of Ace Combat has always been in its flying, when the infinite possibilities of the skies above intersect with the limitations of your aircraft and the realities of your mission. You could play with the standard controls, which substantially limit your aircraft, but you should absolutely play with the Expert scheme if you can. The joy lives in the complete control of the pitch, roll, and yaw of your plane, simultaneously opening you to rapturous moments of aviation choreography and shattering mistakes when you misjudge a turn or your altitude resulting in a devastating crash.

You find yourself in small moments: in the high-G turns to evade incoming missiles, locking onto a group of planes with a special anti-air weapon and knocking four of them out of the sky at once, or deftly weaving through a city and over debris. Wings of Theve captures the fighter pilot fantasy when you're getting on a target's six and downing them with a perfectly placed series of machine gun shots or in finding just the right air speed to stay behind a massive transport before turning your nose and shredding its engines with your guns without ever firing a missile.

It expertly weaves its story, gameplay, and mission design together.

You can be perfect in Wings of Theve if you try, and that's when pilot and aircraft merge and flight becomes an extension of human expression in spite of the limitations of weight and gravity. Each moment and small choice builds the future of your sortie in real time. It's in tailing a Sotoan plane, your reticle turning red, the lock on tone roaring in your ears, and launching a missile and watching it arc elegantly into the other plane’s fuselage before flying through the wreckage in search of your next target. Destruction as beauty. Wings of Theve consistently delivers on this thrill, and it is exhilarating each time.

But what is remarkable is how Wings of Theve marries these moments with its mission design and story. Sometimes, you’ll have your targets marked for you, but often it's on you and the rest of Joker Flight to figure out where to be. Maybe your radar is jammed, and you can’t track the transport planes you need to shoot down, so you’ll need to pick out the contrails they leave behind among the clouds and follow them. Or perhaps a ground detachment is under attack, and calls for aid on your radio. You’ll have to figure out where that detachment is, what you need to target to help, and how to approach it. Can they hold position for a minute while you handle threats elsewhere? Do you dispatch Joker Flight to help, authorizing the use of their limited special weapons, or keep them flying close formation to cover you and try to do it yourself? Missions in Wings of Theve change constantly, and your objectives will change depending on the state of the battlefield. It is a brilliant, graceful ballet where new dancers constantly take the stage, and you must improvise the steps accordingly.

My favorite missions put the ball in Joker Flight’s court. In one, we had to fight off a Sotoan land battleship (think a battleship with tank treads). As we dodged fire from its massive railguns, we also had to cover our ground troops and take out its weapons. It was a tough fight; I’d brought bombs that excelled at destroying its weapons but struggled when we needed precision targeting near the armor around its treads. In another mission, we had to take out airships that helped Sotoa target its Tonitrus Spears. They were hidden in the clouds and invisible from radar, so between fending off air attacks on the Endurance’s fleet, we would follow the massive lasers that guided the Spears once the airships aimed at their targets, and destroy them before they annihilated our fleet.

All of this is brilliant stuff that tests not only your ability to pick the right aircraft and weapons for the job – though you could stick with the capable default F/A-18C, just not as impressive as my beloved F-22A, for example. But it's also about responding on the fly to dynamic objectives that may be very different from your original briefing and the mission you’d planned for. I’ve stuck mostly to talking about the first half of Wings of Theve’s 30 missions here to avoid spoilers, but every single one is excellent, and the final missions pull out all the tricks for some genuinely showstopping moments.

Wings of Theve’s narrative triumph is in portraying most of its drama through the calls coming in over your comms. When your forces are taking heavy losses, some soldiers will urge their comrades to fight on because the Wings of Theve is protecting them, while others will question your usefulness or if the stories about you are even true. You’ll hear men and women die in combat because you weren’t fast enough or just couldn’t protect them. Joker and Queen Flights will react to what’s happening in real time. “Hello traitors, did the wicked get their rest?” Tasha will taunt a former FCU squadron now fighting for Sotoa. Coster will play music to inspire the rest of the crew, and you may end up flying with the guys who recorded it. Sotoan forces will come through on your radio, calling out for their friends as you shoot them down, talking strategy, or taunting you. And then the Shadows themselves might announce their presence by singing over an open channel – that’s when you know you’re in for a serious dogfight (I still can’t get that tune out of my head).

All of this combines with standard combat chatter, but it’s never overbearing as you’ll always know what’s happening. It’s a remarkable achievement in audio mixing, and more impressive that Wings of Theve manages to tell a compelling, emotional story this way. Like previous games in the series, Wings of Theve is a melodrama, and that might turn some folks off, but I found it exceptionally compelling and full of pathos. It’s most effective in its smallest moments – when Tasha confronts the cost of her pacifism, or when Coster gets to meet his musical heroes in the skies. And it extends to just the banter between the crew that fills the quiet moments before or after a mission.

Some of my favorite moments in Ace Combat 8 are when there’s no fighting.

When we had to listen to FCU ground forces calling for help and reporting their losses, wondering aloud if Wings had abandoned them, I felt bad. Keeping them safe was my responsibility, but much of what happens in any given mission is out of your control, no matter how well you fly. That’s war, but it always made me try harder, fly better, and refocus. I had to live up to the legend, whether it was true or not. And while shooting down Sotoan forces and watching them realize they had no chance in real-time was satisfying, it was easy to understand their anger over what had happened to their comrades or their fear when we turned the tide. As exhilarating as being a fighter pilot is, Wings of Theve never lets you forget that everything happening here is a tragedy. And it doesn’t shy away from portraying the toll of war not just on the people forced to fight it, but on civilians who live through it, too. There is a cost to all of this, and the storytelling drives that home every time it can. And yet, you can’t help but want to be everything the Wings of Theve are cracked up to be, to instill hope for desperate people fighting for their right to live free of oppression. Every time I climbed into the cockpit, Wings of Theve reminded me that I was a symbol, more powerful than any combination of pilot or plane could ever aspire to be. The challenge was to live up to it.

Some of my favorite moments in Ace Combat 8 are when there’s no fighting: flying through immaculately rendered clouds, drops of rain speckling my canopy, or landing on the Endurance or at an airstrip after a job well done, or unlocking a new plane and watching the massive hanger doors open and light spill across its sleek lines for the first time. There’s something beautiful about skimming the clouds and basking in the sun in a sky free of missiles and machine gun fire. While you can replay missions and aim for higher scores and S-ranks like me, Ace Combat is kind enough to let you fly around any map peacefully once you’ve completed its associated mission. Cope understood that feeling; maybe it’s why he never shot anyone down. And the longer I played Ace Combat 8, the more I understood him. Maybe he had it right all along.

If the campaign soars, multiplayer is just a pleasant flight… provided you can get it off the ground at all. I like the modes, particularly Deathmatch and the PvPvE mode Co-op Warfare, though I only got to play the former pre-release; it is bizarrely unavailable right now, at least for me. The latter pits two squadrons of four against one another while dotting the map with computer-controlled air and ground enemies, and challenges you to outscore the other team. Do well enough individually and you'll be marked as an ace, which means more points for the other team if they shoot you down. It's fun to form single-match rivalries with other players, even if they're the Red Baron to your Snoopy, but I also like that you can contribute even if you’re not the greatest pilot by taking out your robotic foes.

If you don’t want to deal with other players shooting you down, Co-op Assault is basically the same thing without any of the PvP violence. It’s still fun and a good way to fly more relaxed, friendly skies. Besides, Team Deathmatch is where the real aces fly if you are looking to get sweaty, and you'll learn very quickly when another team is better than you.

The time-limited modes might be my favorites. Emergency Sortie is a standout, pitting an eight-player squadron against superweapons from past games – that could be Ace Combat 7's Alicore, which is a submersible aircraft carrier (this is Ace Combat: things get goofy), or the Chandelier, a massive railgun platform for AC6. My teams have never beaten either, but we've come close, and learning how to fight these behemoths and improving each time made me want to get right back in there for another run. You can’t just jump into them any time, instead randomly earning access to them after playing Co-op Assault or Co-op Warfare, but getting another shot feels like winning a small sweepstakes you didn't realize you'd entered.

Win or lose, you'll earn in-game currency to purchase and upgrade your planes, as well as experience for () the battle pass. There are plenty of daily and weekly challenges to get you what you need without having to spend real money to buy more (which you can do, because we live in The Bad Place), but it still annoys the hell out of me that this is the form these systems take at all – especially because, just like in Ace Combat 7, progression is an issue. The default F-4E plane you start with is lousy, and while you can get a much better (and more familiar to anyone who plays the campaign) F/A-18C pretty quickly, leveling up your plane with blueprints and getting parts for it is a slog (doubly so if you want something nice like the F-22 or F-35).

It never feels great to go into a match and lose because the other team has better aircraft and special weaponry than you do, and I often wished I could just choose what I wanted and get airborne without being forced to deal with unlocks and a progression system. We used to make multiplayer games, man.

I wish I could just choose what I want and get airborne without dealing with unlocks.

The menus are also confusing and kind of a mess. Every option is nested underneath some other option and it's not always clear where you need to go or what menu you need to be in the first place. Even putting together a party and joining a game can be a pain because everyone has to ready up for a mode individually, instead of just having the party leader select it and go. Halo 2 solved these problems in 2004, and we’re still chasing it 20 years later. Once you're in a match, it typically works great and cross-platform play is smooth, but I've also experienced several crashes and disconnects. This baby flies beautifully if you can get off the runway, but sometimes it feels like you’re dodging debris while you're trying to throttle up.

I really like the 100-player lobbies, too. You can head to the arcade and play classic Namco games like Galaga and Dragon Spirit while you wait for a match, or chill and watch someone else play on a big screen. And if you don’t want to sort through AC8's Russian nesting doll menus, you can just walk over to a friendly NPC and get where you need to be. It's also just fun to see other peoples’ customized pilots. I'm sure some folk will wish this was just a menu, but I found this to be a tasteful spice on an already solid dish. I dig it.

So do I wish Wings of Theve's progression system and menus were better? Absolutely. Do I wish it didn't have upgrades and currency and a store, and instead there was a way to just pick a cool plane and fly through the friendly (or unfriendly) skies? You'd better believe it. But I can still see this becoming a place where I spend a decent chunk of time, too. The engines on this old bird might rattle and whine, but she'll get you where you need to go – and it’s all incredibly easy to ignore if you’re just here for the exceptional campaign anyway.

items.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4 Finale Recap and Review - Back to the Future!
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Putting aside the promise of a title like “Tomorrow’s Enterprise” – which obviously echoes the all-time-great Next Gen episode “Yesterday’s Enterprise” – as well as any fan hopes for a Captain Seven from Star Trek: Picard showing up with the crew of the Enterprise-G (yes, some folks were holding out for that unlikely team-up), the Season 4 finale of Strange New Worlds is an enjoyable finish to an incredibly frustrating 10-episode run of highs and lows.

Zeroing in on Celia Rose Gooding’s Nyota Uhura, “Tomorrow’s Enterprise” is a time-travel romp that also functions as a sort of preview of this iteration of the USS Enterprise crew’s end – as well as the show’s. While investigating a white hole – “a unique and rare occurrence,” as Uhura says in her log – as well as fending off Scotty (Martin Quinn), who wants to ask his crewmate out on a date, the newly-promoted lieutenant takes a hit to the noggin after the phenomenon unexpectedly erupts with energy. Next thing she knows, she’s hearing Scotty over the comms suffering some kind of deadly accident… but nobody else hears it or believes her. Nobody except… her future self!

Uhura has often proved to be a great lens through which to tell Strange New Worlds stories, first as the young cadet who was just learning the ropes of serving on a starship, all the way through discovering the hard truths of the job (Hemmer, we miss you!) and the sublime moments it can also offer. And Rose Gooding is terrific as always in this week’s episode as she has to play not just the current-day Uhura, but also the Uhura she’ll be in a year’s time.

Speaking of which, Akiva Goldsman and Henry Alonso Myers, the showrunners of Strange New Worlds, have never tried to hide how much they want to tell stories with The Original Series crew – they were planning a spin-off of SNW called Star Trek: Year One, after all. So once again we get a version of the Enterprise where Kirk is now captain. The events of this future timeline are slightly off, since Scotty is dead after the accident that happens in the past, but you gotta figure it’s mostly correct? I think? If you’re willing to take that leap, then we know Pike has less than a year left before he becomes an admiral and Kirk takes over, Ortegas (Melissa Navia) is going to leave the ship to become a flight instructor, and La’An… well, she’s not around anymore, but nobody wants to talk about it. It’s all a tantalizing tease for how Strange New Worlds end.

As for the romance between Uhura and Scotty that’s happening in the future timeline, it’s funny how this show keeps going back to the Star Trek V: The Final Frontier well. And I’m here for it! That movie – which used to be considered one of the worst of the original crew’s films, though I think that take has softened over the decades (I love it, flaws and all) – did allude to a romantic relationship between the two characters, but it never went beyond that. And really, it’s never made sense that the crews of these starships aren’t hooking up more. Plus, Rose Gooding and Quinn have plenty of chemistry and charisma. Here’s hoping Strange New Worlds keeps pushing this particular final frontier next season.

However, the problem “Tomorrow’s Enterprise” faces is how everything is wrapped up, with the white hole (and black hole on the other side of it in the future timeline) turning out to be some kind of space baby-producing galactic phenomenon that we can’t hope to truly understand… but which tidies up all the problems Uhura has faced for the past hour in a that really puts the in the .

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

  • Scotty checking his breath before he talks Uhura. You know you’ve been there!
  • Uhura pretending to not hear Scotty ask her out. You know you’ve been there!
  • Aha, a Gary Mitchell reference! I just was wondering a couple of weeks ago what happened to (Rong Fu), who was often at the helm of the Enterprise in previous seasons. But also, it was always weird to have a Mitchell sitting there since we knew that Gary Mitchell would eventually take that position – the Gary Lockwood character who was Kirk’s best friend and turned into a god-like being in the first William Shatner episode of TOS, “Where No Man Has Gone Before.” Now we know Jenna and Gary are step-siblings… and have the same job, I guess?
  • Bones also gets a mention here, as he apparently serves as a medical officer alongside Dr. Boyce in the future timeline while Dr. M’Benga is off on Vulcan. This lines up with M’Benga eventually being a Vulcan expert on TOS, but it still doesn’t account for where Dr. Mark Piper is (the doctor in that same first episode with Shatner).
  • Man, the Enterprise has suddenly got all kinds of aliens walking around. I spotted a member of the cat-like species, the Caitians (M’Ress in live-action!?), a bird-like Aurelian, some kind of reptilian dude who was hanging out with a shirt on but no pants like Donald Duck, and some others too. Who was your favorite?

items.title: Absolute Batman #24 Review
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
To hear them tell it, Scott Snyder and Nick Dragotta still have years' worth of stories they want to tell on Absolute Batman. But you almost wouldn't know it from reading the series' current story arc. "The Straw Man" is so crammed full of new characters and key plot twists that it almost feels like the creators are trying to leave it all out on the floor before bidding readers farewell. At times, this arc has threatened to crumble under its own massive weight, but issue #24 is able to keep all those plates spinning while adding in yet another key Bat-character for good measure.

The big news with Absolute Batman #24 is the debut of Absolute Batgirl. Dragotta even pays a lovely tribute to the now-iconic cover of issue #1 with his latest cover image:

Readers should keep their expectations in check as far as Batgirl's role in this issue is concerned, however. She's more a secondary element rather than the main focus of the issue. Mostly, it's just nice to see the series establishing a new heroine and putting a win in Bruce's column after bombarding him with pain and misery for the entirety of this story arc.

That really gets to the heart of Absolute Batman #24's appeal. There's been so much darkness fueling the series of late, from the apparent but not actual death of Martha Wayne to Batman being framed for multiple murders to Bruce being hit with the realization that his entire existence may have been orchestrated by the Joker. This deep into "The Straw Man," it's really vital that the series give readers (and Bruce himself) reason to feel hope. Absolute Batman has been so adept at transforming Scarecrow into a metaphor for our current age of fear and paranoia, but we need to be reminded that good still has a chance of triumphing over fear and despair, even in this twisted universe.

Accordingly, issue #24 is great about exploring Bruce at his lowest ebb and forcing him back into the light. All of the secondary characters and plot threads - Deathstroke and the Robins, Bruce's former friends-turned-villains, etc. - take a backseat to the core tale of Batman getting his Bat-groove back. We're treated to a very satisfying showdown between Bats and Scarecrow, as the series finally acknolwedges that there are limits even to the latter's unnatural power.

Absolute Batman Vol. 1: The Zoo (Hardcover)

Mind you, this is still a very densely packed story, with many supporting characters and the series continuing to emphasize multiple parallel time periods and points of view. As ever, this series only works when the creative team are fully in sync with one another. Dragotta is adept at taking Snyder's complex script and making it digestible on the page. It's never hard to follow the script, even as it bounces between locations and time periods. It helps that Frank Martin's colors draw such a clear distinction between past and present.

Issue #24 is also a terrific showcase for Dragotta's character designs. I love the visual approach to Two-Face here and how Dragotta makes use of the character's long hair and manga-inspired appearance. The Batgirl design is also a very different, very satisfying overhaul to a familiar character. But best of all this month is Scarecrow himself, as we see just how distorted and inhuman this villain can become. Thanks in no small part to Dragotta's art, this character is terrifying in a way he rarely is in other Batman comics.

Unfortunately, as dense as this issue is with plot points, some elements are inevitably going to feel shortchanged. The flashback storyline is the main victim in Absolute Batman #24. The saga of Bruce's short-lived tenure as a mob enforcer reaches a critical point here, and while it mirrors the main storyline nicely, it would have been great to see this plot thread play out in greater depth. That's especially felt once it becomes clear that Snyder and Dragotta are putting their own spin on one of the most iconic Batman moments of all time.

items.title: Slow Horses Season 6, Episode 2 Review — ‘Daddy Issues’
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This review contains full spoilers for Season 6, Episode 2, which is streaming on Apple TV now.

The thing we knew was happening from the first and only Season 6 trailer has happened: Olivia Cooke’s Sidonie Baker has popped back into the picture. The reappearance of the short-lived slow horse was hardly anything — that single “hello, River” line before the end credits roll — and yet raises so many questions. How is she alive? Why has she been in hiding? Why was she playing the spoof-call “triangulation” game with River? What’s she doing in his dead grandad’s house? Most importantly, why did Apple TV spoil this in the trailer?

It’s tough not to imagine how much more of an impact Sid’s return would have had if it had been saved for a jaw-dropping tag at the very last second of this episode. (I’m jealous of those who look at the internet less than me; and yes, I have reconciled with the fact that . Have I learned an important lesson about the true meaning of “Moscow rules”? Probably not.) Regardless, it’s a welcome comeback for a beloved character, despite her only appearing in literally three episodes of Season 1, and it added a fun last flourish to an episode that was already cruising.

As one slow horse enters the picture, another one leaves — poor Moira (Joanna Scanlan) was crossed off the list of the mysterious killers (Kyle Soller and MyAnna Buring). She may have escaped Slough House, but the asterisk on her file would never be deleted. Though we still know very little about who this duo is and why they’re taking out agents who might as well be dead to the Park, something is obviously off. “Seems too easy,” says Buring’s character. “Are you sure we have the right list?” At least now Coe (Tom Brooke) and Shirley (Aimee-Ffion Edwards), in their unlikely yet effective team-up, have picked up the pair’s scent after investigating the house boat of their dead colleague. Even though we’re supposed to hate this horse-murdering pair, their brief characterization across these two episodes has done a ton to up their intrigue points — details like Buring being picky about the goopy soup she’d burn on Moira’s stovetop to cover up the murder and Soller holding Moira’s limp hand as he clicks through TV channels.

This entire episode, “Daddy Issues,” is packed with moments like that — Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) barking at River; River mimicking shooting a projectile in the back of Roddy’s (Christopher Chung) head; Roddy talking about how bitcoin is about to “pop off”; Lamb teasing the Park archivist (Parchivist?) Molly (Naomi Wirthner) about her slay-queen, glam-rock outfit. Actually, this episode was especially stuffed with zesty Lambisms. Taking these extra beats to add a punchline to deeply serious situations is part of the Slow Horses appeal, and Season 6 has once again demonstrated that this is the house style, not something that left with show creator Will Smith after Season 5.

Speaking of deeply serious: We now know that River’s dad Frank Harkness (Hugo Weaving) is maybe at least somewhat involved with the Slough House erasure at the Park, commissioning (and then killing) the Dog who nabbed those files from the records archive. But he’s left a witness, presumed to be a kid, to the murder and has the go-ahead to take care of it. Meanwhile, Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas) is not having the best time as First Chair now that she knows where the money she accepted from Peter Judd (Samuel West) came from and was blackmailed into a sit-down TV interview with the “very slightly right-leaning,” as Judd undersells it, news outlet Talkpoint. (Was that the first time we’ve ever seen Diana caught totally flat-footed?)

“Daddy Issues” is yet another Slow Horses episode that makes spinning a bunch of carefully managed plates look easy. But I’m cognizant of the time crunch; Season 6 has already burned through two episodes, and for as exciting as they are, all of these blank spots need to be filled in so that this web of intrigue doesn’t end in a jumbled mess.

items.title: Brothers Season 1 Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
The first two episodes of debut on Apple TV on September 23.

Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson are great actors, and the last time they made a series together — the first season of True Detective — it was a triumph. It sure is nice to know that they’re such good friends in real life (friends are great!), but Apple TV’s attempt to capitalize on all of this history via their on-screen reunion in Brothers is a misguided endeavor.

In the new series, McConaughey and Harrelson play themselves, kicking off with Woody and his family going to visit Matthew and his family in Texas. The big hook here — based on something the actors have in fact theorized as a possibility in real life — is that in this fictionalized version of these two celebrities’ lives, Woody discovers he and Matthew might be biological half-brothers thanks to an offhand comment from Matthew’s mom (Holland Taylor).

If you were to lean into the weirdness, you could no doubt deliver something genuinely funny and clever with this basic setup, and we’ve certainly seen some great films and series in which celebrities portray skewed versions of themselves. But Brothers feels notably paper thin in terms of its approach, and doesn’t even fully embrace its premise by examining how this friendship might change thanks to this news. Instead, Woody keeps the potential brother revelation a secret from Matthew, relegating his attempts to find out the truth to a background subplot for the majority of the episodes. The actual bigger ongoing storyline is Matthew deciding to run for Governor of Texas and asking Woody to stick around and help with his campaign, which is never that compelling.

McConaughey and Harrelson co-created Brothers along with two accomplished writers, David West Read (& Juliet, Schitt's Creek) and Lee Eisenberg (The Office, Jury Duty), with Eisenberg serving as showrunner. Yet from the start, even with the talent involved, it feels like a struggle to sustain the show for even these eight episodes, resulting in some odd shifts along the way and a tangible feeling that those making Brothers were never sure exactly what kind of show this should be.

As far as depicting these guys as an onscreen comedy duo, initially McConaughey is very much given the straight man role, with Woody as his wacky buddy who keeps getting them into trouble, much to Matthew’s chagrin. While the fact that these two guys are famous isn’t ignored, it’s not front and center to them as characters in this series. But then, halfway through the season, there’s a tangible shift where they’re both now depicted as equally clueless celebrities, blind to how the non-acting achievements they like to boast about mainly happened because they were already so well known.

There's a tangible feeling that those making Brothers were never sure exactly what kind of show this should be.

There is some simple charm in seeing these two bounce off one another in Brothers’ early episodes, but even that begins to dissipate as time goes on and things get sillier, including plotlines like Matthew and Woody dressing in wacky disguises to perform at a local coffeehouse to prove people will like their (bad) music regardless, or something as notably tired and sitcom-hacky as a “Matthew and Woody both forgot to get their wives Valentine’s Day gifts” episode.

As you might expect, Matthew and Woody definitely know how to play Matthew and Woody well, and of course they have good chemistry together, but it’s rarely being used in an interesting manner. However, as much as it feels strange to portray Matthew McConaughey as relatively straitlaced at all — this is a guy who was once arrested after getting high and playing the bongos naked in the middle of the night after all — the early episodes do give him the strongest acting spotlight of the series, as he does good work playing fictional Matthew’s introspection regarding his late father.

But that brings up a strange feeling that also hangs over this series, which provides Matthew and Woody with fictionalized wives (Natalie Martinez and Brittany Ishibashi play Valentina McConaughey and Joy Harrelson respectively), children (played by a group that includes Oona Yaffe, Highdee Kuan, Nolan Almeida, Ella Grace Helton, and Noah Carganilla), and parents (Holland). Again, this kind of thing has been done before, often successfully; Curb Your Enthusiasm did it for years! But it feels off in Brothers because the show doesn’t have a strong point of view. While there are some laughs, it’s never consistently funny, leaving too much time to ponder real life vs. what’s onscreen. For example, frequent mentions of Woody’s dad — vaguely described in the Brothersverse as a deadbeat jailbird — open a can of worms to the dark and violent crimes committed by the actual Charles Harrelson, which is a whole other thing entirely.

Was there a more fearless and subversively funny way to tackle or deflect from this and other messier aspects of these guys’ lives within the show? Absolutely, but Brothers always goes for the safest and tamest route, and it’s only occasionally entertaining enough to make up for that.

items.title: Garfield - Escape from Monday Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
If there are two things to know about Garfield, it’s that he loves lasagne and he hates Mondays. So, it should come as no surprise that developer OSome Studio’s rendition of Jim Davis’s beloved cartoon series, Garfield - Escape from Monday, is heavily bound to those two themes. Set across a series of foodie nightmare worlds, this 3D platformer sees the famous tabby kicking veggies and chomping processed snacks to awaken from a fibre-fuelled fugue state. Sadly, like other disappointing cartoon adaptations (such as SpongeBob SquarePants: The Patrick Star Game), this exploration of the food-obsessed feline’s psyche is actually rather dull. Its overly familiar platforming and excessively camera-winking writing make it little more than a dazzling but sarcasm-laden slog.

Escape from Monday kicks off with a toon-shaded Garfield haphazardly shoveling a slice of what he thinks is Jon’s lasagne into his gullet. Once he realizes the meal is actually laden with veggies, he quickly passes out and is transported to an inner world called the Dreamland, which conveniently takes the form of a board-game course reminiscent of Super Mario Galaxy 2. Here, a vegetarian TV chef, knowingly named Monday, has transformed his cheese-and-meat fantasies into approachable, obstacle-filled levels, stocking them with aggressive snacks to boot. With a kick, a jump, and a forward boost in your arsenal, plus a forgiving health bar, you run Garfield through these stages to eventually wake him up.

The story rarely dives deeper than this initial premise, and leaves you with little more to chew on than "bad food is yummy" and "veggies are gross." I’m not looking for Shakespeare, but it does feel like a wasted opportunity considering how much personality Garfield has in other incarnations (heck, even Bill Murray’s 2004 interpretation had a heart), and how much room there is to have fun with that here. Alas, instead of a sarcastic hero you can root for, Escape from Monday orbits something much worse: an unlikeable cat who delivers a stream of constant complaints until you hit the credits 40-plus levels later.

This one-dimensional attitude grows increasingly grating throughout the roughly 9-hour runtime. Garfield is relentlessly grumbling. When he’s not lamenting his situation, he’s waxing lyrical about the developers, pointing out how certain obstacles or puzzles are repetitive and uninteresting. When his friends appear like expository force ghosts, he continues to disparage them, too. Parading as a PG-13 Deadpool, the meta-humour gradually begins to feel like an excuse, his hypercritical lens intending to lower my own expectations rather than make me laugh.

The most disappointing part of Escape from Monday is the platforming itself.

As you work your way through the zany levels, you’ll also collect hunks of lasagna that fuel a metagame where you furnish a surreal version of Jon Arbuckle’s apartment. To unlock physical versions of sofas and lampshades, you need to find slices hidden in each level, whilst simultaneously gathering enough snacks to fill an on-screen pressure gauge called the Yum-o-meter. While this technically provides extra goals beyond simply reaching the end, the system ultimately feels like an afterthought, so disconnected from the main game it’s easy to forget about his fantasy apartment altogether – I know I did.

Thankfully, the art style provides a much-needed distraction. Escape from Monday’s aesthetics are delightful, evoking the blocky simplicity of PS1 platformers like Rugrats: Royal Ransom. The Dreamland is split into three themed overworlds – Veggie Nightmare, Sweet Kingdom, and the Barbecue Desert – with each featuring a basic, bullet-hell-lite miniboss to defeat as you bounce toward an edible point of interest. By fusing confectionery with familiar adventure tropes like pirates, farmers, and the western frontier, Escape from Monday cleverly conjures the tone of the classic comic strips. Particular standouts include spinning radish stepping stones, Twizzler grind rails, and ketchup-dressed french fries poking out of rocky mountainscapes.

As you wade deeper into each level, the obstacles also evolve nicely, moving beyond basic wooden platforms and bouncy pillow blocks. Suddenly you have to contend with floating panels of meat that flip with your jumps while angry cobs of corn hurl kernels at your head, as well as giant metal graters that launch you into the air as fire-breathing chilli peppers shower you with flames. The combinations were never enough to make me break a sweat, particularly as one hit will take out nearly any enemy, but you can at least feel the deliberate care behind their placement, and I enjoyed the spectacle nonetheless.

Unfortunately, where the levels steadily build, the tools you're given to tackle them aren’t quite as compelling. You eventually uncover thematic outfits that grant you unique powers: There’s a Turkey costume that lets you fly temporarily, beachwear that equips you with a surfboard to ride over bodies of water and skate over obstacles, and cowboy garb that supplies you with a lasso to grapple onto horseshoes to swing over ravines. These additions are far from imaginative, and instead of letting you experiment, Escape from Monday is more keen to explicitly tell you when and where to use them. As such, you’re left mindlessly moving towards the finish line for the sake of… completing the level. The only difference now is that you’re wearing a funny hat.

Still, beyond that lack of any real room for experimentation, the most disappointing aspect of Escape from Monday is the platforming itself. Unlike the grounded movement of It Takes Two or Astrobot, the process of getting Garfield to jump between ledges or kick a rogue zucchini feels more like wading through honey. Sure, the ginger cat is infamous for his overt laziness, but the sluggish action here is at odds with the puzzles around him, and as a result I frequently overshot ledges or prematurely course-corrected due to delayed actions. In early levels, where movement is little more than riding wind gusts or jumping between slowly rotating windmills, it's easy to overlook. But as the obstacles expand, those unearned mistakes started to get under my skin, particularly as I pushed toward the end.

It’s an issue made worse by the erratic camera, with Escape from Monday frequently leaving it unclear who’s in control of your field of view. During the tutorial, you’re given the impression you’ll have the freedom to rotate its position, but during the actual levels after that, the view snaps and twists at random – frequently right in the middle of tricky maneuvers. On many occasions, while planning my next steps, I encountered an irritating camera icon trapped inside a block, indicating that (for whatever reason) I couldn't look around the area. With no alternative, the only option was to ignore my inner explorer and continue down the main path.

The saving grace here is that Escape from Monday is at least extremely generous with its checkpoints. Every few steps, your spot will be saved, allowing you to pop back into place ready to try again if you slip off the map. As with the collectibles, the checkpoints feel more like a band-aid, intended to make the experience is totally frictionless rather than actually solving the platforming issues this game so clearly has. They certainly kept me from getting too frustrated, but in doing so, they also distanced me from the actual joy of progress or success.

items.title: Heart of the Beast Review: Brad Pitt and His Combat Dog Go Ruffin' It in the Wild
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
The lead actor in the new survival drama Heart of the Beast possesses rugged, movie star good looks, does almost all his own stunts, and delivers an understated, deeply moving performance. Brad Pitt is also in this movie. Pitt’s great here, too, but the titular heart of this gripping and emotional film is the dog, who is a very, very good boy indeed.

The movie even opens on the soulful face of Odin (real name Uber), a former US Army combat dog who bears scars, has titanium in his mouth, and a prosthetic leg from injuries suffered in war. His handler/owner is James Belmont (Pitt), a now-retired Green Beret whose face we don’t clearly see until a few moments into the film. As much as James is the protagonist, the film is largely seen through the eyes of Odin.

James and Odin also both suffer from PTSD due to their combat experiences (yes, ). But they have each other, and the bond between them is stronger than steel, a mutual devotion and dependence that keeps them going after James’ plane crashes during a camping trip in the remote wilds of Alaska.

After suffering a heart attack while piloting his Cessna, James is put through the wringer as he and Odin (aka Odie) battle the elements, the terrain, and the wildlife over the next several days as they hike roughly 50 miles to reach the nearest road and get help.

Assuredly directed by David Ayer from a heartfelt screenplay by Cameron Alexander, Heart of the Beast throws nearly every survival scenario possible at James and Odin. From the unrelenting challenges of navigating the land to enduring gnarly injuries to storms to wolves and a grizzly bear, James and Odin encounter everything that could kill you in the woods except for a masked, machete-wielding serial killer.

I was emotionally invested in every moment of their brutal journey because of their relationship. There are as many “please don’t make me cry” moments in Heart of the Beast as there are “God, that looks excruciating” ones, with both James and Odin coming to each other’s aid to help them survive (although, in truth, the dog is pretty useless when it comes to setting up and breaking down campsites!).

Heart of the Beast isn’t as overtly emotionally manipulative as you might expect from a dog movie, simply letting Odin’s face and reactions do the work. But Brad Pitt also makes their whole dynamic work so well because of his deeply human performance. As tough and quiet as James is, his wounded soul and world-weariness are made clear just by Pitt’s eyes. That‘s some damn fine eye acting there, Brad Pitt, especially in the film’s closing moments.

And in a career that’s seen him get famously battered and bloodied in films like Fight Club, Snatch, Mr. and Mrs. Smith, Bullet Train, Fury, and , to name a few, Brad Pitt gets the absolute shit kicked out of him for about three-quarters of Heart of the Beast’s run time. I can’t imagine just how physically grueling this shoot must have been for him.

Less effective are all the flashbacks to James and Odin’s combat experiences, not because they are poorly done but because they don’t convey much new information to the viewer. How both James and Odin ended up with their physical and psychological torments was made perfectly clear during a brief scene with a retired miner (J.K. Simmons) whom they encounter before the plane crash. The flashbacks could’ve been pared down, as they do tend to occasionally interrupt the flow. It’s a testament to how much I cared about James and Odin that I wanted the film to cut back to them and not leave me hanging.

Finally, on a technical level, I need to shout out the sumptuous landscape porn cinematography by Mauro Fiore and the haunting score by Jared Michael Fry. However, the CGI wolves and grizzly bear stick out like sore thumbs (although they’re nowhere near as bad as the CG dog in Call of the Wild). I understand the practical reasons why they had to be used, but the attention they draw distracts from the otherwise very realistic look of the film.

items.title: The Love Hypothesis Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
The Love Hypothesis streams exclusively on Prime Video starting September 23.

Sometimes a rom-com isn’t just a rom-com; such is the case with The Love Hypothesis, a Prime Video movie adaptation of author 2021 New York Times bestseller. In most cases, that’s a cut-and-dry scenario. However, Hazelwood’s book evolved out of the author’s frustration with how the Star Wars sequels turned out; she, among many, was so frustrated with how the characters of Rey and Kylo Ren/Ben Solo were done dirty in Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker that she “fixed” their outcomes through a creative outpouring of fan fiction. One of them was rewritten as The Love Hypothesis and published, turning into an international BookTok sensation and now a movie.

Hazelwood’s book evolved out of the author’s frustration with how the Star Wars sequels turned out.

Why all the history? Because The Love Hypothesis has been created with a decidedly modern lens, depending on the audience watching it. For everyone who just enjoys an entertaining rom-com or loved the book, The Love Hypothesis is an accessible, charming watch led by the warm chemistry of the entire cast, especially leads Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman. For anyone who comes to it from Star Wars fandom and has followed the journey of Hazelwood and her story to this moment in time, the movie is a very meta wink filled with easter eggs tailored just for them.

The basic story remains the same: Third-year Stanford University PhD student Olive Smith (Reinhart) is overworked and underfunded in the traditionally male-dominated science world. Her lifeline through it all is best friend Anh (Rachel Marsh), a fellow PhD student who has pulled Olive out of her shell, introduced her to other friends like Malcolm (Jaboukie Young-White), and become her ride-or-die found family. When Jeremy (Nicholas Duvernay), Olive’s one-time crush, shows interest in Anh, Anh won’t do anything about it because their girl code is stronger than mutual attraction. Olive lies that she has a new boyfriend to get Anh to pursue Jeremy, but that backfires when Anh wants in-person details about Olive’s “date,” and a panicked Olive kisses the first man she sees for cover — the departmental Kylo Ren, Dr. Adam Carlsen (Bateman). What starts as a horribly awkward moment becomes a mutually agreed upon ruse between Olive and Adam when he shares that his grant money is under threat of not being released. Stanford is worried that Carlsen is a flight risk to another research institution, so he could use a “girlfriend” to make it seem like he’s got roots and won’t be exiting anytime soon.

For both audiences, their public relationship-proving moments escalate into more awkward expressions of intimacy, such as suntan lotion applications and recounting their fictional “meet-cute” to his colleagues. Wisely, director Claire Scanlon (The People We Hate at the Wedding) allows these scenes to breathe, heightening their comedic potential and allowing the ensemble to bring out the laughs, of which there are many. Marsh and Young-White are particularly good at pitch-perfect reactions or zingers that lean into the silliness of the “fake dating” scenario while also building a little ecosystem of friendship that drives why Olive is doing what she’s doing.

Reinhart and Bateman also absolutely sell the thawing between these two socially awkward dorks into a genuine romance. Yes, in reality they’re both too pretty to ever have that descriptor applied to them, but as Olive and Adam, you buy why they’d hold the world at arms’ length and decide not to do so with one another. Comedically, they’re top notch, and the scenes where they get to express genuine honesty and mutual loneliness with one another percolates into a friendship and bubbling attraction that’s the do-or-die element to any great rom-com.

The STEM-centric aspects of the story are watered down in Sarah Rothschild’s script, though an homage sequence to Martha Coolidge’s 1985 science comedy, Real Genius, very much works as it adds a sense of color and context to Olive’s world. Less successful is the science villain of the piece, who gets a lot more time to unfurl his machinations in the book. Here, he isn’t given enough story real estate to be as potent an adversary, or to even rise above a one-note character with clichéd intentions. Fortunately, Rothschild’s screenplay replaces that screen time with more consequential scenes for Olive and Anh, the bedrock for why this “fake dating” operation is even happening. Portraying the strength of their bond is far more worthwhile, underpinning the romantic story with a deeper one about friendship and sisterhood.

At its heart, The Love Hypothesis is a gentle satire of romance tropes, especially enemies-to-lovers, and a celebration of female friendship.

And for the fans who go all the way back to this story’s Star Wars origins, there are a wealth of easter eggs to find and laugh over, from pointed needle drops to very specific Laura Karpman musical character themes, and even red-and-blue color cameos. The production knows who you are, and they’ve clearly got a sense of humor and respect for the OG fandom.

At its heart, The Love Hypothesis is a gentle satire of romance tropes, especially enemies-to-lovers, and a celebration of female friendship. Both sound potentially hokey, but this mostly female creative team understands what made the book a hit and knew how to translate it here. They let the tone be earnest yet firmly tongue-in-cheek, and allow their cast to weave their magic — especially Reinhart and Bateman — giving rom-com lovers the exact chemistry that makes the genre work.
